Read this email from your English-speaking friend Alex and the notes you have made.

***
From: Alex
Subject: Your new course!

I'd love to know if you are enjoying it. Is the teacher nice? [Great!]

Maybe I can join you next time. When is the next class? [Answer]

Alex

questions.explanation: To get a high score in B1 Writing Part 1, make sure you answer all four notes clearly: 1) Tell Alex what kind of course it is (e.g., photography, cooking, Italian). 2) Confirm that you are enjoying it and that the teacher is great. 3) State when the next class is. 4) Suggest a specific day (Saturday or Sunday) to meet up. questions.question:

You see this notice on an international English website for young people:

LEARNING SOMETHING NEW
What is a new skill you would like to learn? Why do you want to learn it? Is it easy or difficult for young people to learn new things?

Write your story.

questions.explanation: The man says he feels "so much fitter" and the woman replies "Me too", adding that she sleeps better and has more energy. They disagree about money (she spent a fortune on the bike) and about speed (it is slower for her but faster for him).

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a TV series. Why did the woman stop watching it?
options: a) She found the story confusing.
b) She didn't like the actors.
c) She didn't have enough time.
questions.explanation: She says there were so many characters and it kept jumping in time, so "I had no idea what was going on, so I gave up". She thought the actors were good ("brilliant") and she had plenty of time on holiday.

questions.question: You will hear a girl phoning a friend. Why is she calling him?
options: a) To change their arrangement
b) To ask to borrow something
c) To invite him to the cinema
questions.explanation: Lucy asks "could we go to the nine o'clock one instead?", so she wants to change the time they arranged. She says she doesn't need to borrow his bike any more, and the cinema trip was already planned, so it is not a new invitation.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a new phone. What does the woman think about it?
options: a) It is difficult to set up and use.
b) It cost more than she had expected.
c) The camera is disappointing.
questions.explanation: She says the photos are "nothing like the ones in the adverts" and come out "dark and blurry", and she feels "let down". It cost less than she expected and she says it is "really simple to use".

questions.question: The club's new facility is an indoor ______.
questions.explanation: The coach says "we've built an indoor climbing wall". Many members hoped for a swimming pool, but it was too expensive, so the pool is not the answer.

questions.question: Beginners' classes will take place on ______ evenings.
questions.explanation: The classes "will be on Thursday evenings from seven till eight thirty". Tuesday was the original plan, but the hall is busy then.

questions.question: Climbers must bring their own ______.
questions.explanation: The coach says "please bring your own water bottle". The club lends shoes and gives out helmets, so climbers do not need to bring those.

questions.question: People who join before the end of May will receive a free ______.
questions.explanation: The coach says anyone who joins before the end of May "will get a free sports bag". The free T-shirt was last year's offer.

questions.question: To book a place on a class, go to ______.
questions.explanation: The coach says "you'll need to go to reception". The website is not working properly yet, so members should not book there.

questions.question: In July, volunteers are needed to help with the ______.
questions.explanation: The coach says "we still need people to help with the fun run through the park". The summer barbecue is already organised by the parents' committee.

questions.question: Why did Helen decide to become a park ranger?
options: a) She wanted a job with a good salary.
b) She was tired of living in a big city like London.
c) A childhood experience inspired her.
questions.explanation: Helen says it "goes back to when I was about ten", when a ranger took her school group to look for badgers and she thought "that's what I want to do". She says she loved living in London and that money isn't the reason anyone becomes a ranger.

questions.question: What does Helen find most difficult about her job?
options: a) Working very long hours during the busy summer
b) Dealing with visitors who ignore the rules
c) Working outside in the wind and rain in winter
questions.explanation: She says "What I find really difficult is when visitors leave rubbish or let their dogs chase the sheep" and she is not comfortable telling people off. She enjoys stormy days and doesn't mind the long summer hours.

questions.question: How does Helen feel about the increase in visitors to the park?
options: a) Pleased that more people are enjoying nature
b) Annoyed that the hills have become crowded
c) Worried that it will damage the paths
questions.explanation: Helen says "Honestly, I'm delighted" because so many people have discovered the outdoors. It is her colleagues who worry about the paths, and she says the hills are never really crowded.

questions.question: What is Helen's opinion of the technology rangers use?
options: a) It helps, but can't replace local knowledge.
b) It costs the park far too much money to use.
c) It means that fewer rangers are needed now.
questions.explanation: She says the cameras and app "save us loads of time", but "a camera can't tell you why the deer have moved" and "You still need someone who really knows the land". She says they don't cost as much as people think.

questions.question: What does Helen advise young people who want to become rangers to do?
options: a) Get a job in a visitor centre first
b) Do some voluntary work in a park
c) Study for a university degree
questions.explanation: She says "The best thing is to volunteer" because it is the only way to find out if you love the work. She says a degree isn't essential and that you don't learn much about the land in a visitor centre.

questions.question: What does Helen say about her future?
options: a) She would like to train new rangers.
b) She plans to work in another country.
c) She wants to stay in the job she has now.
questions.explanation: Helen says "I'm happy right where I am" and hopes to still be there when she retires. She turned down the job training new rangers and decided against Canada because she would miss the park.

questions.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) The self-service tills do not accept payment by card.
b) Customers paying with cash should go to the customer desk.
c) Customers who want to pay in cash must use a different till.
questions.explanation: The notice says the self-service tills take 'card payments only' and that people who 'wish to pay with cash' should 'use the staffed tills near the main entrance', so cash customers need a different till. The customer desk is only mentioned for gift vouchers, not cash, and the self-service tills do accept cards — in fact they accept only cards.

questions.question: What does the label tell customers?
options: a) The bread is baked fresh in the store twice a day.
b) Bread still on the shelf in the evening costs less.
c) Staff can keep cheaper bread for you to pick up later.
questions.explanation: The label says 'Anything left on the shelf at 6 p.m. is reduced to half price', so bread bought in the evening is cheaper. Reduced items 'cannot be put aside for customers to collect later', so staff will not keep them for you, and the bread is baked 'every morning', not twice a day.

questions.question: Why is Sam's mum sending this message?
options: a) To find out where the shoe shop has moved to
b) To arrange to meet Sam at the cinema on Saturday
c) To ask if Sam wants her to buy some trainers today
questions.explanation: Mum asks 'Shall I buy the blue pair in your size now, or would you rather choose yourself on Saturday?', so she wants to know if she should buy the trainers today. The shoe shop 'has closed down'; it has not moved. The cinema is only mentioned to say where SportZone is, and Saturday is when Sam might choose the shoes, not a meeting at the cinema.

questions.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) Parking is free for two hours with a shop receipt.
b) Anyone can park in the car park for two hours without paying.
c) Drivers have to pay at the machine as soon as they arrive.
questions.explanation: The first two hours are free 'if you show a receipt from any shop in the centre', so only people who have bought something park for free. Without a receipt 'the normal charge of £2 per hour applies', so parking is not free for everyone, and the receipt is shown at the machine 'before you leave', not on arrival.

questions.question: What does the sign say about trolleys?
options: a) You may take a trolley home if you leave £1.
b) You will get your money back when you return the trolley.
c) You must return the trolley to the place where you got it.
questions.explanation: The sign says 'Your coin comes back when you return the trolley', so you get your £1 back. Trolleys must not be taken 'out of the car park', so you cannot take one home, and you can return it 'to any trolley park', not only the one where you got it.

questions.question: Laura would like to learn to take better photos, but she only has a mobile phone. She works every Saturday, and she would like someone to comment on her pictures after the course has finished.
options: A) Street Photography Day
B) Painting in the Hills
C) A Taste of Italy
D) Kitchen Basics
E) Photos with Your Phone
F) Pottery Weekend
G) Write Your Own Songs
H) The Home Story Club
questions.explanation: Photos with Your Phone is on Sunday, teaches people to use 'the camera on their mobile phone', and 'after the course, you can send your photos to the teacher by email and get personal advice'. Street Photography Day is also about photos, but it is on Saturday, when Laura works, and you must 'bring your own digital camera, as phones are not suitable'.

questions.question: Tom has hardly ever cooked, and he would like to learn together with his twelve-year-old daughter. They are only free on Saturday mornings.
options: A) Street Photography Day
B) Painting in the Hills
C) A Taste of Italy
D) Kitchen Basics
E) Photos with Your Phone
F) Pottery Weekend
G) Write Your Own Songs
H) The Home Story Club
questions.explanation: Kitchen Basics is 'for families to learn together', accepts 'children aged ten and over' with an adult, is for people who have 'never cooked before' and takes place on Saturday morning. A Taste of Italy is also a cooking class, but it is on Sunday afternoon and is for people who 'already feel confident in the kitchen'.

questions.question: Maria has been cooking for years and wants to learn to make dishes from another country. She doesn't eat meat, and she prefers learning in a small group where the teacher has time for everyone.
options: A) Street Photography Day
B) Painting in the Hills
C) A Taste of Italy
D) Kitchen Basics
E) Photos with Your Phone
F) Pottery Weekend
G) Write Your Own Songs
H) The Home Story Club
questions.explanation: A Taste of Italy is for people who 'already feel confident in the kitchen', teaches 'real Italian home cooking', has 'no more than eight students' so 'everyone gets plenty of attention', and 'several dishes are made without meat'. Kitchen Basics is also about cooking, but it is for people who have 'never cooked before' and does not teach food from another country.

questions.question: James wants to try painting for the first time and doesn't own any equipment. He would like to spend the whole weekend outside, and he enjoys walking.
options: A) Street Photography Day
B) Painting in the Hills
C) A Taste of Italy
D) Kitchen Basics
E) Photos with Your Phone
F) Pottery Weekend
G) Write Your Own Songs
H) The Home Story Club
questions.explanation: Painting in the Hills is a 'two-day course' that 'takes place entirely outdoors', includes a walk of 'about three kilometres' each morning, needs 'no experience', and 'all paints, brushes and paper are provided'. Pottery Weekend also lasts two days, needs no experience and provides everything, but it is held 'in our bright studio', not outside, and it is not painting.

questions.question: Sophie loves writing and wants to improve her stories. She has a young baby, so she can't leave the house, and she would love to see her writing printed one day.
options: A) Street Photography Day
B) Painting in the Hills
C) A Taste of Italy
D) Kitchen Basics
E) Photos with Your Phone
F) Pottery Weekend
G) Write Your Own Songs
H) The Home Story Club
questions.explanation: The Home Story Club can be done 'from your own home' by video call, is about 'short stories', and 'the best stories are printed in a small book'. Write Your Own Songs is also a writing course, but it is held at the Riverside Arts Centre, so Sophie would have to leave the house, and the songs are performed, not printed.

questions.question: Why did the writer's parents begin to feel better about her plan?
options: a) Several of her friends were going on the same project.
b) She promised to find a job when she came back.
c) She had already saved enough money for the trip.
d) They learnt that the organisation had a long history.
questions.explanation: The writer says that 'when I showed them that the organisation had been running for over twenty years, they began to feel more relaxed about it'. Her parents wanted her to 'get a job and save money instead', but she never promises to do this, and her friends 'went straight to university', not to the project.

questions.question: How did the writer feel about living at the campsite?
options: a) She never really got used to the heat and the insects.
b) She wished she had had her own room for the whole stay.
c) She found it difficult at first but later came to enjoy it.
d) She was pleased to be camping again after many years.
questions.explanation: She says 'the first week was hard', but 'I soon got used to it, and by the end I actually preferred sleeping outside'. She had 'never been camping before', so she was not camping again, and she says she soon got used to the conditions, so she did not miss her own room for the whole stay.

questions.question: What does the writer say about the tourists on the beaches?
options: a) Many of them wanted to find out more about the turtles.
b) Most of them were unhappy that some of the beach was closed.
c) They often damaged the nests with their chairs and umbrellas.
d) Very few of them paid attention to the volunteers' signs.
questions.explanation: The writer says 'Most visitors were very interested and asked lots of questions'. Only 'a few were annoyed that part of the beach was closed', not most of them, and she never says that tourists damaged nests or ignored the signs.

questions.question: Why was the writer frightened the first time she worked at the information stand?
options: a) She had to give a talk to a large group of children.
b) The other volunteers had left her there on her own.
c) She did not know enough facts about sea turtles.
d) She could only say a few words in the local language.
questions.explanation: She was 'terrified the first time because my Greek was limited to "hello" and "thank you"'. She only gave talks to children later, 'by August', and 'the other volunteers helped me', so she was not left alone.

questions.question: What advice does the writer give to people who are thinking of volunteering?
options: a) Learn some of the local language before you leave.
b) Check carefully what you will be expected to do.
c) Go with a friend so that you do not feel lonely.
d) Choose a project in a place that looks beautiful.
questions.explanation: Her advice is to 'Find out exactly what the work involves, and make sure it's something you really care about'. She warns people not to choose a project 'just because it looks good in photos', and she does not advise learning the language first or going with a friend.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
options: a) put
b) kept
c) stayed
d) spent
questions.explanation: 'We stayed at a youth hostel' is the normal way to say where you slept during a trip. 'Put', 'kept' and 'spent' all need an object (you put or keep something; you spend time or money), so 'We put/kept/spent at a youth hostel' is not correct.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
options: a) watch
b) look
c) view
d) see
questions.explanation: When you point your eyes in a direction, the verb is 'look': 'too nervous to look down'. 'See', 'watch' and 'view' are not used with 'down' in this way.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
options: a) changed
b) went
c) moved
d) became
questions.explanation: 'The weather changed suddenly' makes sense, and it explains why they 'got completely wet'. 'Became' and 'went' need a word after them (became cold, went grey), and weather does not 'move'.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
options: a) at
b) by
c) in
d) on
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'on the way back', meaning during the journey back to the hostel. 'In the way' has a different meaning (blocking someone), and 'at the way' and 'by the way' do not mean 'during the journey'.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
options: a) made
b) did
c) caused
d) got
questions.explanation: The structure is 'make someone do something': Leo 'made everyone laugh'. 'Caused' and 'got' need 'to' before the verb (caused/got everyone to laugh), and 'did everyone laugh' is not correct here.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
options: a) advise
b) recommend
c) tell
d) persuade
questions.explanation: You 'recommend something to someone' when you say it is good: 'I would definitely recommend it to next year's students'. We 'advise' and 'persuade' people, not things ('advise it to' and 'persuade it to' are wrong), and 'tell it to' would mean repeating a story.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (1).
questions.explanation: After a superlative with the present perfect we use 'ever': 'the best job I have ever had'. 'Never' would give the opposite meaning and is not possible after 'the best'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (2).
questions.explanation: The adjective 'responsible' is always followed by 'for': 'I was responsible for a group of twelve children'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (3).
questions.explanation: The relative phrase is 'most of which': 'their activities, most of which were outdoors', meaning that most of the activities took place outside.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (4).
questions.explanation: The structure 'so + adjective + that' shows a result: 'I was so exhausted that I fell asleep before the children did'. 'Such' is used before a noun, not an adjective alone, and 'too' cannot be followed by 'that'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (5).
questions.explanation: 'One of the' is followed by a superlative and a plural noun: 'one of the happiest children'. By the end of the camp Callum was very happy, which contrasts with how he cried every night in his first week.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (6).
questions.explanation: The time expression is 'as soon as', meaning 'immediately when': 'As soon as applications open again, I'm going to apply'. No other word can come before 'soon as' here.

questions.question:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Jamie and the notes you have made.

From: Jamie
Subject: My visit!

Hi!

Great news: I've booked my ticket, and I'm coming to stay with you for the weekend next month! [Note 1: Brilliant!]

I'll arrive on Friday evening. Is it better for me to get a taxi from the station to your house, or can you meet me? [Note 2: Explain]

What do you think we should do on Saturday? I'd love to see the best places in your town. [Note 3: Suggest...]

Also, what should I bring? I've no idea what the weather will be like. [Note 4: Tell Jamie]

See you soon,
Jamie

Write your email to Jamie using all the notes. Write about 100 words.
questions.explanation: A good answer is an informal email of about 100 words that covers all four notes: 1) reacts positively to the news of the visit; 2) explains how Jamie should get from the station (for example, that you will meet Jamie there, or how to get a taxi or bus); 3) suggests one or more things to do in the town on Saturday, with a reason; 4) tells Jamie what to bring, mentioning the weather. It should have a suitable opening and closing (Hi Jamie / See you soon), use linking words (because, so, but) and a range of B1 language such as suggestions (Why don't we..., We could...) and future forms (I'll..., It's going to...).

questions.question:
Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question A: Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for young people.

Articles wanted!
A day out in my town
Where would you take a visitor for a perfect day out in your town? What would you do there, and why would they enjoy it?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Question B: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence:

When I opened the door, my friend was standing there.

Write your story.
questions.explanation: Article: a good answer has an interesting title, speaks directly to the reader, answers all three questions in the notice (where to go, what to do, why a visitor would enjoy it) and gives personal opinions and reasons, in about 100 words. Story: a good answer begins with the given sentence, continues clearly from it with a beginning, middle and end, uses past tenses correctly (past simple, past continuous, past perfect), and includes some description of feelings, with linking words such as then, suddenly and in the end.

questions.question:
The examiner asks you some questions about yourself, travel and holidays. Answer each question with two or three sentences.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. How do you usually travel to school or work?
3. Where did you go on your last holiday?
4. Do you prefer holidays by the sea or in the mountains? Why?
5. Tell us about a place in your country that you would like to visit.
questions.explanation: A good answer gives more than one word: it answers each question directly and adds a reason, example or extra detail (for example, "I usually go by bus because it's quicker than walking"). It uses the past simple correctly for the last holiday, comparatives or preferences (I prefer..., I'd rather...) for the sea or mountains, and would like to / I'd love to for the place to visit.

questions.question: Look at the photograph. It shows a family on holiday in a small harbour town by the sea. There are colourful houses along the water, boats in the harbour, and the family is sitting at a table outside a café, looking at a map. Tell us what you can see in the photograph. You have about one minute.
questions.explanation: A good answer describes the scene for about a minute: the place (a harbour, houses, boats), the people (who they are, what they are wearing, what they are doing), and the weather or atmosphere. It uses the present continuous (They're looking at a map), there is / there are, and prepositions of place (in the background, on the left, next to). If the candidate doesn't know a word, they paraphrase ("a kind of small boat for fishing"). Good candidates also guess or give an opinion (They might be planning their day; It looks like a relaxing place).

questions.question:
Your class has won a prize: a one-day trip together. Here are some places you could go.

a city with museums and shops
a beach
a theme park
a national park for walking
a farm where you can help with the animals

Talk together about the different places and say which would be the most fun and interesting for the whole class. Then decide which place is best. You have about two or three minutes.
questions.explanation: A good performance discusses several of the options with reasons (cost, travel time, weather, what everyone in the class would enjoy), makes suggestions (What about...? Why don't we...?), agrees and disagrees politely (I see what you mean, but...), asks for the partner's opinion (What do you think?), and works towards a decision together (So shall we choose...?). Candidates do not need to agree, but they should try to reach a decision.

questions.question:
The examiner asks you and your partner some more questions about travelling. Give your opinion and reasons, and respond to what your partner says.

1. Do you prefer going on holiday with your family or with friends? Why?
2. Is it better to plan a trip carefully or to decide things when you get there?
3. What was the best trip you have ever been on? What made it special?
4. Do you think people should travel less by plane? Why or why not?
5. What can people learn from visiting other countries?
questions.explanation: A good answer gives an opinion with reasons and examples, not just yes or no. Candidates use the present perfect for experiences (The best trip I've ever been on...), phrases for opinions (In my opinion..., I think...), and react to their partner (Do you agree? That's a good point). Longer answers that develop an idea are better than short ones.

questions.question: What will the man have for lunch?
options: a) A cheese sandwich on brown bread
b) A plate of chicken salad
c) A bowl of tomato soup with bread
questions.explanation: The man says "I'll just have a cheese sandwich, please" and chooses brown bread. The chicken salad is finished, and he doesn't want the tomato soup because he had it at home last night.

questions.question: How much does the woman pay for the pizzas?
questions.explanation: The normal price is eighteen pounds, and the woman thinks it will be sixteen, but the man explains it is "two pounds off each pizza, not the whole order. So you only pay fourteen."

questions.question: What did the girl forget to buy?
options: a) A carton of milk
b) A packet of butter
c) A box of eggs
questions.explanation: The girl has brought the milk and "the big box of eggs", but when her mum asks about the butter she says "Oh no, I knew there was something" and has to go back to the shop for it.

questions.question: Where will the friends eat tonight?
options: a) In a burger bar
b) In an Italian restaurant
c) At home
questions.explanation: The Italian restaurant is "fully booked until Saturday" and there is nothing in the fridge to cook at home, so they agree on "the burger bar near the station": "Good idea ... Let's go at about seven."

questions.question: What time does the café stop serving breakfast today?
questions.explanation: Breakfast stops at eleven only from Monday to Friday; "at weekends we carry on until half past eleven" and today is Saturday. Twelve o'clock is when the lunch menu starts.

questions.question: What does the woman order to drink?
options: a) A cup of tea
b) A glass of orange juice
c) A large coffee
questions.explanation: The orange juice is not available because the machine isn't working. She first says she'll have tea but then changes her mind: "Could I have a coffee instead? A large one, please."

questions.question: Which dessert does the waiter recommend?
options: a) Apple pie with ice cream
b) A slice of chocolate cake
c) A bowl of fruit salad
questions.explanation: The waiter says the chocolate cake is popular but "quite heavy" and the fruit salad is "nothing special"; then he says "If I were you, I'd have the apple pie", which comes with ice cream.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a new shopping centre. What does the woman think about it?
options: a) It is difficult to find a place to park there.
b) It is too busy and crowded at weekends.
c) The shops are the same as in other towns.
questions.explanation: She says the shops are "the same big chain stores you find in every town" and she was hoping for "something a bit different", so she was disappointed. It was not crowded ("actually it was fine") and parking "was great".

questions.question: You will hear a man talking to a friend about a jacket. Why is he taking it back to the shop?
options: a) Part of it is damaged.
b) It is the wrong size.
c) He paid too much for it.
questions.explanation: He says "The zip's broken already, and I've only worn it twice." The size is not the problem because "it fits me perfectly", and the price is not the problem because it was "a real bargain" in the sale.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a market they visited. What do they agree about?
options: a) The food was the best thing there.
b) The clothes were of poor quality.
c) The market was smaller than they expected.
questions.explanation: The woman says "the food stalls were amazing" and the man replies "Absolutely. They were the best thing there." They disagree about the clothes (the woman found a lovely scarf), and the woman says the market was "much bigger" than she expected.

questions.question: You will hear a girl talking to her father. What does she want to do in town on Saturday?
options: a) Buy the new phone in a shop there
b) Find a cheaper price for it online
c) Look at a phone before she buys it
questions.explanation: She says "I'm not going to buy it in the shop"; she just wants "to see it properly first, and hold it in my hand" to check the size. She will order it online later at home, not in town.

questions.question: You will hear two neighbours talking about their local post office. How does the man feel about the new opening hours?
options: a) Annoyed
b) Pleased
c) Surprised
questions.explanation: He says the change "makes such a difference to me" because he can now go on his way home from work instead of queuing on Saturdays. He is "Not really" surprised, and the Saturday closing "doesn't matter to me any more", so he is not annoyed.

questions.question: You will hear a woman recommending a hairdresser to a friend. Why does she like it?
options: a) You can go there without booking ahead.
b) The staff pay attention to customers' wishes.
c) It is cheaper than other hairdressers.
questions.explanation: She likes it "Because they actually listen to you. They ask exactly what you want before they start cutting." It is "about the same" price as everywhere else, and you have to book "at least a week ahead".

questions.question: This year the festival will take place in ________.
questions.explanation: The presenter says the festival used to be in the town square, but "This year, though, it's moving to Castle Park".

questions.question: The main stage will be next to the ________.
questions.explanation: Last year the stage was next to the car park, but "This time you'll find it next to the lake".

questions.question: On Saturday afternoon children under twelve can enter a ________ competition.
questions.explanation: The painting competition "won't be happening this year"; instead "there's a cake decorating competition on Saturday afternoon for anyone under twelve".

questions.question: Visitors are advised to bring a ________ to sit on.
questions.explanation: There will only be a few chairs, so "the organisers suggest that you bring a blanket to sit on". Umbrellas should not be brought.

questions.question: Tickets are cheaper if you buy them ________ before Thursday.
questions.explanation: Tickets cost twelve pounds at the entrance, "but if you buy them online before Thursday, you'll only pay eight pounds".

questions.question: The best way to get to the festival is to take the ________ from the railway station.
questions.explanation: Parking is limited and taxis will be expensive, "So the best thing to do is to take the shuttle bus from the railway station."

questions.question: How did Lucy feel when she first started swimming?
options: a) Bored by the lessons at the pool
b) Excited to be doing the same sport as her brother
c) Frightened of one part of swimming
questions.explanation: Lucy says "I was terrified of putting my face in the water." It was her brother who was keen, not her, and the lessons "were fun" because the teacher turned everything into a game.

questions.question: What does Lucy say about training early in the morning?
options: a) She has come to enjoy it.
b) It is the hardest part of her routine.
c) It makes her feel tired at school.
questions.explanation: She hated the alarm at first, "But now I actually love it." She says the evenings are harder, and at school she is "more awake than anyone".

questions.question: Why did Lucy change coaches?
options: a) She wanted to focus on a different kind of race.
b) Her first coach did not have enough experience.
c) Her first club was too far from her home.
questions.explanation: Her first coach "mainly worked with sprinters", but Lucy realised she "was better at longer races", so she joined a club that specialises in distance swimming. The coach "had loads of experience" and the old club was "just round the corner".

questions.question: How does Lucy feel now about her result at last year's national championships?
options: a) She believes she was unlucky.
b) She is still annoyed with herself about it.
c) She thinks it helped her to improve.
questions.explanation: She says "it was the best thing that could have happened, because I'm much faster now", after working on her slow starts. She was only disappointed "for a day or two", and she rejects the idea that she was unlucky: "that wasn't really it".

questions.question: What is Lucy's opinion of using social media?
options: a) It puts too much pressure on young athletes.
b) It is a good way to encourage other people.
c) It takes up too much of her time.
questions.explanation: The best thing for her is when girls join a swimming club "because they watched my videos" - "That makes it all worth it." She only posts once a week, so it "doesn't take up much time", and although some swimmers talk about pressure, she says "I don't feel that at all".

questions.question: What advice does Lucy give to young swimmers?
options: a) Check your progress against other swimmers.
b) Make sure you enjoy what you are doing.
c) Look for the best club you can find.
questions.explanation: She says "The most important thing is to make sure you're having fun." She tells them not to worry about "finding the perfect club" and not to "compare yourself with other swimmers all the time".

questions.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) You can buy cold food this week, but not hot meals.
b) The café is looking for new staff for its kitchen.
c) The café will be completely closed until next Monday.
questions.explanation: The notice says 'Hot meals will not be available until Monday, but you can still buy sandwiches, cold drinks and ice creams'. The café is not closed, because the counter is still selling things, and the problem is a repair, not a lack of staff.

questions.question: What is the new rule at the swimming pool?
options: a) Children under 8 can get a pool card from reception.
b) Young children may not swim without an adult.
c) All children must swim with an adult at all times.
questions.explanation: The notice says 'children under 8 must have an adult with them in the water at all times'. It is not all children, because 'older children may swim on their own', and the pool card is for these older children, not for children under 8.

questions.question: Why has Sam written to Leo?
options: a) To explain why they need to meet earlier than planned
b) To cancel their game because there are no courts free
c) To ask Leo to book a court at the sports centre
questions.explanation: Sam has booked a court at the sports centre, which is 'further away', so Sam suggests meeting 'at 9.30 rather than 10' – earlier than planned. The game is not cancelled, and Sam has already booked the court ('I've reserved one'), so Leo does not need to do it.

questions.question: What does the sign say about dogs?
options: a) They cannot come into the park between April and July.
b) They must be kept on a lead everywhere in the park.
c) They are not allowed in certain parts of the park.
questions.explanation: Dogs are welcome 'in all areas of the park except the children's playground and the flower garden', so there are some parts where they cannot go. Between April and July they can still come in, but must be on a lead only 'near the lake', not everywhere.

questions.question: What is the sports centre telling people?
options: a) The Tuesday yoga class has moved to Thursday.
b) Places in yoga classes can now be booked by phone.
c) There is now an extra yoga class every week.
questions.explanation: The centre says 'we have added a second class on Thursdays', so there is one more class each week. The Tuesday class has not moved – the new class is in addition to it – and places 'cannot be reserved by phone'.

questions.question: Maria wants to read a true story about a journey. She reads on her phone on the train to work and would like something she can finish in a week or two.
options: A) Murder at Kingsbridge Station
B) Two Wheels, One World
C) Cheap and Cheerful Cooking
D) From Garden to Table
E) Small Space, Big Harvest
F) Walking Home
G) The Cat Who Solved Crimes
H) Max Moves In
questions.explanation: Walking Home is a 'true account' of a twelve-day walk, is 'only 150 pages long' and is 'an e-book, so you can download it straight to your phone'. Two Wheels, One World is also a true story about a journey, but it is 'over 600 pages' and 'only available as a large hardback', so Maria cannot read it on her phone.

questions.question: Tom has just moved into his first flat and doesn't have much money for food. He wants to learn to make simple meals and likes to see pictures of how to do every stage.
options: A) Murder at Kingsbridge Station
B) Two Wheels, One World
C) Cheap and Cheerful Cooking
D) From Garden to Table
E) Small Space, Big Harvest
F) Walking Home
G) The Cat Who Solved Crimes
H) Max Moves In
questions.explanation: Cheap and Cheerful Cooking is for people 'cooking for themselves for the first time', has 'easy recipes' costing 'less than three pounds a portion' and 'photos showing each step'. From Garden to Table also has recipes, but they are 'impressive recipes for dinner parties' with ingredients 'from expensive food shops', and it has drawings, not step-by-step photos.

questions.question: Hannah is fourteen and loves books that make her laugh. When she enjoys a book, she always wants to go on reading about the same characters in other books.
options: A) Murder at Kingsbridge Station
B) Two Wheels, One World
C) Cheap and Cheerful Cooking
D) From Garden to Table
E) Small Space, Big Harvest
F) Walking Home
G) The Cat Who Solved Crimes
H) Max Moves In
questions.explanation: Max Moves In is 'the funniest book' teenage readers have read this year, and 'it's the first in a series', with more books 'about Max and his cousin'. The Cat Who Solved Crimes is also 'very funny', but 'this will be the only book about Whiskers', so Hannah could not read more about the same characters.

questions.question: David drives a long way to work every day and would like to listen to a detective story in the car. He is especially interested in stories about the past.
options: A) Murder at Kingsbridge Station
B) Two Wheels, One World
C) Cheap and Cheerful Cooking
D) From Garden to Table
E) Small Space, Big Harvest
F) Walking Home
G) The Cat Who Solved Crimes
H) Max Moves In
questions.explanation: Murder at Kingsbridge Station is a 'detective novel' set in '1920s Manchester', with 'details of life a hundred years ago', and there is 'an excellent audiobook version' David can listen to while driving. The Cat Who Solved Crimes is also a detective story set in the past (Victorian London), but 'there is no audio version'.

questions.question: Lucy lives in a flat with a small balcony and wants to grow her own vegetables. She has never done any gardening before.
options: A) Murder at Kingsbridge Station
B) Two Wheels, One World
C) Cheap and Cheerful Cooking
D) From Garden to Table
E) Small Space, Big Harvest
F) Walking Home
G) The Cat Who Solved Crimes
H) Max Moves In
questions.explanation: Small Space, Big Harvest shows how to grow vegetables 'in pots on a balcony or windowsill' and 'assumes you know nothing about plants'. From Garden to Table also explains how to grow vegetables, but 'in a large garden', and it is 'aimed at people with some experience', so it is wrong for Lucy.

questions.question: What happened the first time Leah played outside the station?
options: a) Her friend had to help her when she made mistakes.
b) A child's reaction helped her to feel calmer.
c) She earned less money than she usually did in cafés.
d) She felt so nervous that she stopped early.
questions.explanation: Leah was terrified at first, but 'a little girl stood in front of me and danced through every song, and by the end I'd completely forgotten my nerves'. She did not stop early, her friend only 'dared' her to play, and she earned 'more money than I'd ever earned in a café', not less.

questions.question: What does Leah say about the weather?
options: a) She never plays when the forecast is bad.
b) People give her more money when it is sunny.
c) The council does not allow street music in the rain.
d) Very hot days can be almost as bad as rain.
questions.explanation: Leah says 'Rain is bad, obviously, but a very hot day is almost as bad', because people hurry and do not stop. She checks the forecast 'all the time' but never says she refuses to play, and the council rules she mentions are about volume and time, not rain. She does not say that sunny days bring more money; on very hot days people 'don't want to stand still'.

questions.question: Why does Leah think playing in the street has made her a better performer?
options: a) People who stop often give her useful advice.
b) She has to perform for longer than in a concert hall.
c) People leave at once if they don't enjoy it.
d) She has learnt to play much more loudly.
questions.explanation: Leah says street audiences are honest: 'if you're not good enough, they simply walk away', and 'it has made me a much better performer' because she notices 'when I'm losing people'. She never mentions advice from listeners, and there are rules about 'how loud you can be', so playing louder is not the reason.

questions.question: How did Leah deal with the complaints from the man in the shop?
options: a) She stopped using her speaker in the square.
b) She asked the council to speak to the man.
c) She moved to a different part of the square.
d) She changed the songs she played near his shop.
questions.explanation: Leah understood that 'he had to listen to me all day', so 'Now I play my quieter songs when I'm near his door'. She still plays in the same square with her speaker, and she does not mention contacting the council about him.

questions.question: What would Leah probably say about her future?
options: a) 'Whatever happens, I want to play in the street sometimes.'
b) 'I'm sure that I'll be really famous in a few years' time.'
c) 'As soon as I find a manager, I'll stop playing in the street.'
d) 'I'd much rather record music in a studio than play outside.'
questions.explanation: Leah is 'in no hurry to give up the street', and even if she becomes famous she would 'like to come back to the square now and then'. She says she would not get 'the same feeling in a studio', and she doubts she will become famous ('which I doubt').

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: The writer 'stopped trying to study for hours at the weekend'; the sentence about ending up 'tired and bored' and forgetting everything 'by Monday' gives the reason, and 'Instead, I spent twenty minutes... every single day' follows naturally. The sentence about preferring 'a grammar book on Sunday afternoons' is also about weekend study, but it contradicts the writer's decision to stop.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: The writer needed words for everyday tasks, not colours and animals, 'So I made a list of every phrase I needed'. The next sentence begins 'That list became my first vocabulary book', which refers back to this list. No other sentence mentions a list.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: The writer 'hardly spoke at all', so Rosa 'noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice'. The next sentence, 'She told me that people would be pleased I was trying', refers to Rosa and repeats her advice. No other sentence introduces a woman who could be 'she'.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: 'This' refers to watching films with Portuguese subtitles, which was 'very frustrating' because the writer had 'to pause every few minutes'. The next sentence contrasts with it: 'After a while, though, I found I could follow a whole film without stopping it once.' The sentence about being 'tired and bored' does not fit, because it talks about forgetting things 'by Monday', which only makes sense after weekend study.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (5)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: In the running club 'nobody spoke English', so at first the writer 'could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but 'gradually we started chatting on the long runs'. This leads to 'Now some of those runners are my closest friends'. The sentence saying 'everyone there spoke excellent English' contradicts the text.

questions.question: Gap (1): millions of us ____ our weekly shopping without leaving the house.
options: a) do
b) take
c) have
d) make
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'do the shopping' / 'do our weekly shopping'. We do not say 'make', 'take' or 'have' our shopping in English.

questions.question: Gap (2): before they ____ a decision.
options: a) get
b) make
c) do
d) put
questions.explanation: The collocation is 'make a decision'. 'Do a decision', 'put a decision' and 'get a decision' are not correct English.

questions.question: Gap (3): Lots of people ____ prices on several websites to find the best deal.
options: a) correct
b) confuse
c) compete
d) compare
questions.explanation: To find the best deal, people look at the prices on different websites to see which is cheapest: they 'compare prices'. 'Compete' needs 'with' and is about trying to win, 'correct' means remove mistakes, and 'confuse prices' would not help anyone find a good deal.

questions.question: Gap (4): when shops ____ big discounts.
options: a) earn
b) offer
c) pay
d) spend
questions.explanation: Shops 'offer discounts' to customers. Shops do not 'pay', 'spend' or 'earn' discounts; these verbs are used with money, not with discounts.

questions.question: Gap (5): let customers send items back free of ____.
options: a) money
b) price
c) charge
d) value
questions.explanation: 'Free of charge' is a fixed expression meaning 'without paying'. 'Free of money', 'free of price' and 'free of value' are not used in English.

questions.question: Gap (6): Whoever is right, one thing is ____: the way we shop has changed for ever.
options: a) certain
b) secure
c) safe
d) confident
questions.explanation: 'One thing is certain' means 'one thing is sure to be true'. 'Secure' and 'safe' describe things that are protected from danger, and 'confident' describes people, not facts.

questions.question: Gap (1): I had never lived anywhere bigger ____ our local market town.
questions.explanation: 'Bigger' is a comparative adjective, so it must be followed by 'than' before the thing it is compared with ('our local market town'). No other word can link a comparative to its second part.

questions.question: Gap (2): I was afraid ____ getting lost, so I carried a map everywhere.
questions.explanation: The adjective 'afraid' is followed by the preposition 'of' + noun or -ing form ('afraid of getting lost'). 'About', 'for' or 'to' do not work before 'getting' here.

questions.question: Gap (3): I didn't know anyone in the city, and neither ____ my flatmate.
questions.explanation: 'Neither + auxiliary + subject' means 'also not'. The first verb is in the past simple negative ('didn't know'), so the auxiliary must be 'did'. 'Was' or 'had' do not match 'didn't know'.

questions.question: Gap (4): Things got better when I found ____ about a climbing club near my office.
questions.explanation: 'Find out (about something)' is a phrasal verb meaning 'discover information'. Without 'out', 'found about' is not correct English.

questions.question: Gap (5): ____ is always something to do, from free concerts in the park to street markets.
questions.explanation: 'There is' introduces something that exists: 'There is always something to do'. 'It is always something to do' is not correct, because 'it' needs something to refer back to.

questions.question: Gap (6): At ____ same time, I can't imagine going back now.
questions.explanation: 'At the same time' is a fixed expression meaning 'but also / however'. 'Same' always takes 'the' in this phrase; 'a same time' or 'this same time' are not used.

questions.question:
You must answer this question. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Read this email from your English friend Sam and the notes you have made.

From: Sam
Subject: Your phone!

Hi,

Good news - I've found your phone! It was under the back seat of my car. You must have dropped it when I gave you a lift home from the cinema on Friday. [Note 1: Great! Thank Sam]

I can bring it round to your house, or you can come and pick it up from mine. Which would be better for you? [Note 2: Explain which and why]

I'm free on Saturday or Sunday this week. When shall we meet? [Note 3: Suggest a day and time]

By the way, how have you managed without your phone for the last few days? [Note 4: Tell Sam]

Sam

Write your email to Sam using all the notes.
questions.explanation: A strong answer covers all four notes in a friendly, informal email of about 100 words: (1) thanks Sam and shows relief or happiness about the phone (e.g. "Thanks so much - I thought I'd lost it for ever!"); (2) says whether Sam should bring the phone or the writer will collect it, with a reason (e.g. "I'll come to yours, because I'm going into town anyway"); (3) suggests a specific day and time (e.g. "How about Saturday at about eleven?"); (4) describes what it has been like without the phone (e.g. "It's been difficult because I couldn't check the bus times"). Assessed on Content, Communicative Achievement (informal register, suitable opening and closing), Organisation (paragraphs, linking words such as because, so, anyway) and Language (range of B1 vocabulary and structures, e.g. past simple, present perfect, suggestions).

questions.question:
Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2 - Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for young people.

Articles wanted!
Technology in my life
What piece of technology do you use most, and what do you use it for?
Could you live without it for a week? Why or why not?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Question 3 - Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
The phone rang at midnight.

Write your story.
questions.explanation: Article: a strong answer has an interesting title or opening that engages the reader, names one piece of technology and explains what the writer uses it for, and answers whether they could live without it for a week, with reasons (e.g. "I couldn't, because I use it to talk to my family abroad"). It may address the reader directly ("Could you manage without yours?"). Story: a strong answer begins with the given sentence, continues in the past tenses, has a clear sequence of events (who called, why, what happened next) and a satisfying ending, with some description of feelings (e.g. "I was so frightened that I couldn't speak"). Both are assessed on Content, Communicative Achievement, Organisation and Language at B1 level, in about 100 words.

questions.question:
Part 1 - Interview

The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer each question with at least one or two full sentences.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. What time do you usually get up on a weekday?
3. Tell us about what you usually do in the evenings.
4. What do you enjoy doing at the weekend?
5. Do you prefer spending your free time at home or going out? Why?
6. Tell us about something you did in your free time last week.
questions.explanation: A strong answer goes beyond one word and adds a reason or an example (e.g. "I usually get up at about seven, because school starts at half past eight"). Candidates should use the present simple with adverbs of frequency for routines (usually, often, hardly ever), the past simple for last week, and expressions of preference (I prefer ... because ..., I'd rather ...). Assessed on Grammar and Vocabulary, Discourse Management, Pronunciation and Interactive Communication.

questions.question:
Part 2 - Photograph

Look at the photograph. It shows a group of people relaxing in a park on a sunny afternoon. In the front, a young family is having a picnic on a blanket under a large tree; a man is reading a book, and a little girl is eating a sandwich. Behind them, two teenagers are throwing a frisbee on the grass, and in the background an older woman is walking her dog along a path next to a small lake.

Tell us what you can see in the photograph. You have about one minute.
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes the people, what they are doing, the place and the weather, and organises the description with expressions of place (in the front, behind them, in the background, on the left/right, next to). Candidates should use the present continuous (are having a picnic, is walking her dog) and can speculate with It looks like ..., They might be ..., I think it's probably the weekend because .... If they don't know a word (e.g. frisbee), they should paraphrase ("a round plastic thing you throw"). Assessed on Grammar and Vocabulary, Discourse Management and Pronunciation; candidates should keep talking for about one minute.

questions.question:
Part 3 - Collaborative task

I'm going to describe a situation to you. A group of friends has a free afternoon next Saturday. They want to do something together, but they don't have much money. Here are some things they could do.

go to the cinema
go for a bike ride in the countryside
play football or basketball in the park
cook a meal together at someone's house
visit a museum in the town centre

Talk together about the different things the friends could do, and say which would be the most enjoyable. Then decide which activity is the best for the group. You have about two or three minutes.
questions.explanation: A strong answer discusses several options with reasons (cost, weather, whether everyone would enjoy it), makes suggestions (Why don't they ...? How about ...? They could ...), responds to the partner (I agree, That's a good idea, but ...; What do you think?) and works towards a decision together (So, shall we choose ...?). Candidates do not need to agree, but they must interact rather than give two separate monologues. Assessed mainly on Interactive Communication, as well as Grammar and Vocabulary, Discourse Management and Pronunciation.

questions.question:
Part 4 - General conversation

Discuss these questions with your partner.

1. What free-time activities are popular with people of your age where you live?
2. Is there a free-time activity you don't enjoy? Why not?
3. Do you think people have less free time now than in the past? Why?
4. Would you like to try a new hobby? What would it be?
5. Is it better to spend free time with friends or on your own? Why?
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives opinions with reasons and examples (I think ... because ...; For example, ...), talks about likes, dislikes and habits (I really enjoy ..., I can't stand ..., I tend to ...), uses would for hypothetical wishes (I'd love to try climbing) and comparatives when comparing now and the past. Candidates should also react to their partner's ideas and ask follow-up questions (What about you?). Assessed on Grammar and Vocabulary, Discourse Management, Pronunciation and Interactive Communication.

questions.question: What does the girl need to take to the school concert?
options: a) a small torch
b) a music stand
c) a folding chair
questions.explanation: The girl says the hall will be dark, 'so we all need a small torch to read our music'. The school already has 'plenty of' music stands, and chairs have been borrowed from the church hall, so she does not need to take either.

questions.question: Where are the Year 9 students going on their trip?
options: a) to a farm park
b) to a castle
c) to a science museum
questions.explanation: The boy says 'We're going to the science museum in the city instead'. The castle was the original plan but the coach company cannot do that date, and the farm park is 'closed until the spring'.

questions.question: Which piece of homework does the boy still have to finish tonight?
options: a) a science poster
b) a history essay
c) a maths worksheet
questions.explanation: The history essay must be on Mr Dean's desk 'first thing tomorrow morning' and the boy has 'only written the introduction'. He has already done the maths worksheet, and the science poster 'isn't due until next Friday'.

questions.question: What time will the first races start on sports day?
options: a) at half past ten
b) at quarter past nine
c) at nine o'clock
questions.explanation: The message says 'the first races will now start at quarter past nine'. Half past ten was the old start time, and nine o'clock is when students should arrive at school, not when the races begin.

questions.question: What did the girl win in the art competition?
options: a) a ticket for a gallery exhibition
b) a book of famous paintings
c) a big box of paints
questions.explanation: The girl says 'This year the winner got a ticket for the new exhibition at the city gallery'. The box of paints was last year's prize, and the book of paintings went to the girl who came second.

questions.question: Where is the parents' evening taking place?
options: a) in the main hall
b) in the dining room
c) in the library
questions.explanation: The woman says 'everyone's in the main hall'. The library is being painted, and the dining room was planned but is 'too small for all the teachers' tables'.

questions.question: What is Josh going to do in the talent show?
options: a) play the guitar
b) do a dance
c) tell jokes
questions.explanation: Josh says 'I'm going to stand up on stage and tell jokes'. He decided not to play the guitar because 'loads of people are doing music', and he is 'definitely not dancing'.

questions.question: You will hear two colleagues talking about their new office. What does the woman think about it?
options: a) It is too noisy with everyone in one big room.
b) It makes it easier to share information.
c) It takes her longer to get there.
questions.explanation: The woman says she can 'just turn round and ask' the design team instead of sending emails, and they have 'sorted out more problems'. She expected noise but says 'actually it's been fine', and it is the man, not the woman, who has a longer journey; for her it is 'about the same'.

questions.question: You will hear two students talking about a part-time job. Why is the boy leaving his job at the café?
options: a) He isn't paid enough.
b) He doesn't get on with his manager.
c) He needs more time to study.
questions.explanation: The boy says his exams start in May and 'I've got so much revision to do that something has to go'. He says the pay is 'quite good' and the manager 'is lovely', so the other reasons are wrong.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about online language courses. What do they agree about?
options: a) The courses are good value for money.
b) The lessons are too long to follow after work.
c) The teachers explain things clearly.
questions.explanation: The woman says 'for thirty pounds a term, you can't really complain' and the man agrees: 'That's true. You get a lot for the price.' They both like the forty-minute lessons, so they do not think they are too long, and both say their teachers do not always explain things well.

questions.question: You will hear a woman talking to her manager. Why has she come to see him?
options: a) To offer to help with some work
b) To ask for some time off
c) To complain about a colleague
questions.explanation: Helen has finished her own work and asks 'if I could join them for a couple of weeks' to help Tom's team with the website. She says 'it's not that' when the manager mentions her holiday, and she mentions that Tom's team is behind only to explain her offer, not to complain.

questions.question: You will hear a girl talking about a job interview. How does she feel about it?
options: a) Worried that she wasn't prepared
b) Pleased with how she did
c) Annoyed that it started late
questions.explanation: The girl says 'it went better than I expected' and 'I really think I've got a good chance'. She was kept waiting but 'didn't really mind', and she had prepared well: 'I'd read all about the museum beforehand'.

questions.question: You will hear a man talking about his university course. What is his opinion of it?
options: a) The lectures are boring.
b) Four years is too long for a course like this.
c) The practical work is the best part.
questions.explanation: The man says that what he loves most is "the time in the workshop", where they build and test things, so the practical work is the best part for him. He does not find the lectures boring, because he says the lecturers make them interesting, and he does not think four years is too long: he says the time goes quickly when you enjoy it.

questions.question: The centre is opening later than planned because the ______ needed more time.
questions.explanation: Kate says 'We were hoping to open in February, but the builders needed a little more time to finish everything.'

questions.question: The part of the centre that the staff are proudest of is the ______.
questions.explanation: Kate lists the pool, the sports hall and the gym, then says 'the thing we're proudest of is our climbing wall'. The other facilities are mentioned but not described in this way.

questions.question: People who join before the opening day get their first ______ free.
questions.explanation: Kate says 'if you join before the opening day, your first month is completely free.' The prices of thirty-two and twenty pounds are the normal monthly costs, not the offer.

questions.question: On Sunday mornings, the pool is only open for ______.
questions.explanation: Kate says 'The pool will be open only for parents and children' on Sunday mornings.

questions.question: The manager recommends that people travel to the centre by ______.
questions.explanation: Kate says the car park 'only has forty spaces, so we'd really recommend coming by bike'. The bus is mentioned, but she points out that it 'only runs once an hour', so she does not recommend it.

questions.question: Free tours of the centre leave from the ______ every afternoon this week.
questions.explanation: Kate says the tours 'leave from the reception desk at four o'clock'. The main entrance is where the bike shelter is, not where the tours start.

questions.question: Why did Leila first become interested in designing games?
options: a) A teacher at school encouraged her.
b) She enjoyed changing the games she owned.
c) She hoped to make a lot of money from it.
questions.explanation: Leila says she 'used to change the levels in the games I'd bought' and 'enjoyed that far more than just playing them'. She says her teachers thought games were 'a complete waste of time' and that she 'certainly didn't expect to get rich'.

questions.question: What does Leila say about her university course?
options: a) It taught her how to work with other people.
b) It did not include enough programming.
c) She wishes she had studied art instead.
questions.explanation: Leila says 'the most useful thing was the group projects' because 'nobody works alone' and she 'learnt to listen to other people's ideas'. She thought about switching to art but says 'I'm glad I didn't', and she found the programming hard, not too little.

questions.question: How did Leila feel about her first job?
options: a) She felt her boss at the small company treated her unfairly.
b) She was bored by the work she was given.
c) She was surprised by how much testing there was.
questions.explanation: Leila says 'I had no idea how much testing goes into a game' and 'I just hadn't expected it'. She says 'It wasn't boring exactly' and that her boss 'was very kind to me'.

questions.question: What does Leila think is most important in a good game?
options: a) Rules that are easy to understand
b) Graphics that look really beautiful
c) An exciting story for the player
questions.explanation: Leila says players will stop playing if they 'can't understand what to do in the first two minutes', 'however beautiful the game looks', so 'simple rules come first'. She says a good story 'helps', but it is not the most important thing.

questions.question: What is Leila's opinion about young people playing video games?
options: a) They should only play educational games.
b) Games are fine as long as they do other things too.
c) Parents should not limit the time children spend on games.
questions.explanation: Leila says games are not bad for young people, but her own children 'have to go outside and see their friends as well' and play for 'an hour or so after their homework'. She does not mind whether games are educational, and she does set a time limit herself.

questions.question: What advice does Leila give to people who want to design games?
options: a) Go to university to study programming first.
b) Get a job testing games before anything else.
c) Start making simple games straight away.
questions.explanation: Leila says 'Don't wait' and 'Make something simple, show it to your friends'. She says 'You don't have to go to university first' and 'you certainly don't need to start as a tester'.

questions.question: Lucy and her husband want a beach holiday with their two children, aged four and six. They want a beach where it is safe for small children to swim, and they would like to cook their own meals. They also need something for the children to do indoors if it rains.
options: A) Glenmore Lakes Campsite
B) Sandy Bay Holiday Park
C) The Seacliff Hotel
D) Valmora Old Town
E) The Hilltop Hotel
F) The Isle of Carra
G) Brenton Harbour Hostel
H) Windy Point Campsite
questions.explanation: Sandy Bay has a beach 'where the water stays shallow a long way out' with lifeguards, 'every caravan has its own kitchen', and 'if the weather turns bad, the indoor play centre offers games, crafts and films for under-tens'. The Hilltop Hotel also has a beach 'perfect for young children', but 'rooms do not have kitchens' and its kids' club is outdoors.

questions.question: Tom wants a quiet holiday away from traffic, where he can spend his days walking in the hills. He is also interested in history and would like to find out about the people who have lived in the area.
options: A) Glenmore Lakes Campsite
B) Sandy Bay Holiday Park
C) The Seacliff Hotel
D) Valmora Old Town
E) The Hilltop Hotel
F) The Isle of Carra
G) Brenton Harbour Hostel
H) Windy Point Campsite
questions.explanation: On the Isle of Carra 'no cars are allowed', 'paths lead over the hills', and the museum 'tells the story of the families who have lived here for over a thousand years'. Glenmore Lakes also has walking paths, but it is 'next to the main road' and says nothing about history.

questions.question: Priya and her friend are students with very little money. They enjoy going out to hear live music at night, and they would like to learn how to cook some local food during their holiday.
options: A) Glenmore Lakes Campsite
B) Sandy Bay Holiday Park
C) The Seacliff Hotel
D) Valmora Old Town
E) The Hilltop Hotel
F) The Isle of Carra
G) Brenton Harbour Hostel
H) Windy Point Campsite
questions.explanation: In Valmora the bars and squares 'fill with live music until the early hours', a hostel bed 'costs just £15 a night', and at the Kitchen School 'local chefs show small groups how to make the region's famous dishes'. Brenton Harbour Hostel is also cheap and has a cookery class, but it warns 'don't expect much nightlife'.

questions.question: Mr and Mrs Gordon are retired and do not want to drive on holiday. They would like to stay in a comfortable hotel where they can relax in a spa, and they want to go out on the water to see wildlife.
options: A) Glenmore Lakes Campsite
B) Sandy Bay Holiday Park
C) The Seacliff Hotel
D) Valmora Old Town
E) The Hilltop Hotel
F) The Isle of Carra
G) Brenton Harbour Hostel
H) Windy Point Campsite
questions.explanation: The Seacliff Hotel has 'comfortable rooms' and a spa, 'guests do not need a car' because a free minibus meets every train, and 'boat trips leave twice a day to watch the dolphins and seals'. The Hilltop Hotel also has a spa, but 'guests will need a car' and it offers no boat trips.

questions.question: Daniel has never tried water sports before and would like to have lessons in sailing or windsurfing. He wants to go camping and take his dog with him.
options: A) Glenmore Lakes Campsite
B) Sandy Bay Holiday Park
C) The Seacliff Hotel
D) Valmora Old Town
E) The Hilltop Hotel
F) The Isle of Carra
G) Brenton Harbour Hostel
H) Windy Point Campsite
questions.explanation: Windy Point Campsite gives 'sailing and windsurfing lessons for complete beginners', you can 'pitch your tent', and 'dogs are very welcome'. Glenmore Lakes is also a campsite with boats, but only 'experienced sailors can hire boats', 'we do not offer lessons' and 'we cannot accept pets'.

questions.question: What does Emma say about her job in the first paragraph?
options: a) It is as exciting as most people think.
b) It is easy to get good photos on most trips.
c) She usually knows exactly when the animals will appear.
d) Most of her time is spent waiting.
questions.explanation: Emma says 'I spend most of my time waiting – sometimes for days'. She says 'the truth is rather different' from what people imagine, so it is not as exciting as people think, and 'on many trips I come home without a single photo I'm happy with', so good photos are not easy to get.

questions.question: What did Emma enjoy about photographing birds as a child?
options: a) Seeing how good her photos were.
b) Learning the names of different garden birds.
c) Having to be patient and silent for a long time.
d) Showing her pictures to her grandfather in his garden.
questions.explanation: She says 'I loved the challenge of staying still and quiet for so long'. Her photos were not good ('Most of the pictures were terrible'), and the text does not mention showing them to her grandfather or learning bird names.

questions.question: How did Emma's career as a photographer begin?
options: a) A scientist sent some of her photos to a magazine.
b) She went to Scotland to take photos for a magazine.
c) Her university teachers told her to study photography.
d) A magazine offered her a job when she finished university.
questions.explanation: On the research trip 'one of the scientists saw my photos and sent them to a nature magazine', which printed three of them. She went to Scotland 'to count sea birds', not to work for a magazine, and she took her camera 'just for fun'.

questions.question: What does Emma think about preparing for a trip?
options: a) Knowing about the animal is more important than having good equipment.
b) She must ask local fishermen for advice before every trip.
c) She needs to buy a more expensive camera for each new animal.
d) She should never plan to stay in one place for more than six days.
questions.explanation: She reads about where the animal feeds and when it is active, and says 'Good preparation matters far more than an expensive camera.' The fishermen in Norway are only one example, and seeing the otters 'on the sixth day' does not mean she limits her trips to six days.

questions.question: What advice would Emma give to a young person who wants to photograph wildlife?
options: a) "Buy the best camera you can afford before you start."
b) "Practise near where you live, and never upset the animals."
c) "Get as close as you can to an animal, even if it seems nervous."
d) "Save up so that you can travel to places like Africa."
questions.explanation: Emma tells young people to 'begin close to home' because 'a local park is full of wildlife', and says 'If it seems stressed, put your camera down and walk away. No photo is worth frightening an animal.' She says 'You don't need to travel to Africa', and earlier that an expensive camera matters less than preparation.

questions.question: Gap (1): I had ____ up running two years earlier because I wanted to get fit.
options: a) got
b) put
c) taken
d) made
questions.explanation: 'Take up' means to start a new hobby or activity: 'I had taken up running'. 'Get up' means to leave your bed, 'put up' means to build or raise something, and 'make up' means to invent – none of them mean starting a sport.

questions.question: Gap (2): I couldn't run for more than ten minutes ____ stopping.
options: a) instead
b) without
c) except
d) unless
questions.explanation: 'Without stopping' means continuously, with no break. 'Unless' must be followed by a clause (unless I stopped), 'instead' needs 'of' (instead of stopping), and 'except stopping' does not make sense here.

questions.question: Gap (3): It was a friend from work who finally ____ me to enter the race.
options: a) persuaded
b) suggested
c) made
d) let
questions.explanation: Only 'persuade' is followed by object + to-infinitive: 'persuaded me to enter'. We say 'suggested that I enter', and 'made' and 'let' are followed by the infinitive without 'to' (made me enter, let me enter).

questions.question: Gap (4): I found a training plan online and ____ my distance a little every week.
options: a) grew
b) rose
c) added
d) increased
questions.explanation: 'Increase' takes an object and means to make something bigger: 'increased my distance'. 'Grow' and 'rise' do not take an object here (my distance rose), and 'add' needs 'to' (added to my distance).

questions.question: Gap (5): On the day of the race, the ____ was amazing.
options: a) atmosphere
b) climate
c) surface
d) nature
questions.explanation: 'Atmosphere' is the feeling created by the people in a place, and the next sentence describes it: people 'clapping and shouting our names' and bands playing. 'Climate' is the usual weather of a region over many years, 'surface' is the top of the road, and 'nature' means plants and animals – none of these are described.

questions.question: Gap (6): I was completely exhausted, but I have never felt so ____ of myself.
options: a) glad
b) proud
c) pleased
d) happy
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'proud of yourself'. 'Pleased' and 'happy' are followed by 'with' (pleased with myself), and 'glad' is not used with 'of myself'.

questions.question: Gap (1): I finally bought one and tried to teach ____ by watching videos online.
questions.explanation: The subject 'I' is also the person who learns, so the verb 'teach' needs the reflexive pronoun 'myself' ('teach myself' = learn without a teacher). 'Me' is not correct when the object is the same person as the subject.

questions.question: Gap (2): My fingers hurt quite ____ lot.
