questions.explanation: 'Quite a lot' is a fixed expression meaning 'very much'. 'Lot' needs the article 'a' here; 'quite the lot' or 'quite lot' are not correct.

questions.question: Gap (3): They weren't strong ____ to press the strings down properly.
questions.explanation: 'Adjective + enough + to-infinitive' says whether something has the necessary quality: the fingers did not have the strength needed. 'Enough' comes after the adjective ('strong enough'); 'too' and 'very' go before it.

questions.question: Gap (4): After a month I nearly gave ____ playing.
questions.explanation: 'Give up + -ing' is a phrasal verb meaning 'stop doing something'. The writer found it hard and almost stopped. 'Gave in' is not followed by an -ing form, and 'gave away' needs an object like 'the guitar'.

questions.question: Gap (5): Apart ____ the technique, she has taught me to read music and to play in a band.
questions.explanation: 'Apart from' means 'as well as / in addition to'. 'Apart' is always followed by 'from' in this expression.

questions.question: Gap (6): I now try to practise for twenty minutes every evening ____ I am working late.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'except if': the writer practises every evening, but not on the evenings when they work late. 'If' or 'when' would mean the opposite (practising only on those late evenings).

questions.question:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Sam and the notes you have made.

From: Sam
Subject: Maya's birthday

Hi!

It's Maya's birthday on the 18th and I'd love us to plan something special for her. [Note: Great idea!]

I was thinking of either a picnic in the park or going bowling. Which do you think she'd prefer? [Note: Say which and why]

I'd also like to buy her a present together with you. Have you got any ideas? [Note: Suggest...]

Could we meet this weekend to organise everything? [Note: Yes, tell Sam when]

Speak soon,
Sam

Write your email to Sam using all the notes. Write about 100 words.
questions.explanation: A good answer is an informal email (e.g. 'Hi Sam', 'See you soon') of about 100 words that covers all four notes: 1) reacts positively to the idea of doing something for Maya's birthday; 2) chooses the picnic or bowling and gives a reason (e.g. 'She'd prefer bowling because she loves games and it might rain'); 3) suggests a present (e.g. a book by her favourite author, concert tickets); 4) agrees to meet and says when (e.g. 'How about Saturday afternoon at the café?'). Content, communicative achievement, organisation (linking words such as because, so, also) and a range of B1 language (would, could, suggestions like 'Why don't we...?') are assessed. Missing a note lowers the Content mark.

questions.question:
Choose ONE of these questions. Write about 100 words.

Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for teenagers.

Articles wanted!
A celebration I will never forget
Tell us about a celebration you will always remember. What were you celebrating? Who was there? Why was it so special?
The best articles will appear on our website.

Write your article.

Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence:

Everyone shouted 'Surprise!' when I walked in.

Write your story.
questions.explanation: Article: a good answer has an interesting title or opening that catches the reader's attention, answers all three questions (what was celebrated, who was there, why it was special), gives some personal feelings or opinions, and speaks to the reader (e.g. 'Have you ever...?'). Story: a good answer begins with the given sentence, has a clear sequence of events and an ending, uses past tenses correctly (past simple, past continuous, past perfect), and includes some description of feelings (e.g. 'I couldn't believe my eyes'). For both, about 100 words; content, communicative achievement, organisation and a range of B1 language are assessed.

questions.question:
Answer the examiner's questions about yourself.

What's your name? Where do you live?
Do you work or are you a student?
What do you enjoy most about your studies or your job? Why?
How do you usually travel to your school, college or workplace?
Tell us about a teacher or a colleague who has helped you.
What would you like to study or do in the future?
questions.explanation: Give full answers, not just one or two words: add a reason or an example (e.g. 'I enjoy biology most because I like learning how the body works'). Use present simple for routines, past simple for the story about a teacher or colleague, and would like / going to / hope to for the future. Grammar and vocabulary, pronunciation and interactive communication are assessed.

questions.question:
Look at the photograph. It shows a group of four young people working together at a large table in a bright office. One woman is pointing at a laptop screen, a man is writing notes on a whiteboard, and two others are looking at papers and smiling. There are coffee cups and coloured sticky notes on the table.

Tell us what you can see in the photograph. Talk for about one minute.
questions.explanation: Describe the people, what they are doing, where they are and what things you can see, using the present continuous ('A woman is pointing at...', 'They're discussing...'). Use there is / there are, prepositions of place (on the left, in the background, next to) and guesses with might / may / looks like ('They might be planning a project'). If you don't know a word, explain it in other words ('small pieces of paper you can stick on things'). Keep talking for about a minute.

questions.question:
A group of students from your school has some free time on Saturday mornings and wants to do a short course together. Here are some courses they could choose:

a cooking course
a first aid course
a computer programming course
a photography course
a course in a foreign language
a course on how to start a small business

Talk together about the different courses the students could do, and say which would be the most useful for them. Then decide which course they should choose. Talk for about two or three minutes.
questions.explanation: Discuss several of the options with your partner before deciding; do not just describe them one by one. Give opinions with reasons ('A first aid course would be useful because you never know when someone might need help'), ask your partner's view ('What do you think?', 'Do you agree?'), agree and disagree politely ('That's a good point, but...') and reach a decision together at the end ('So shall we choose...?'). Interactive communication is especially important in this part.

questions.question:
Answer the examiner's questions and discuss them with your partner.

Do you prefer studying on your own or with other people? Why?
Is it a good idea for students to have a part-time job? Why or why not?
What skills do you think are most important for finding a good job today?
Would you like to work in an office, or somewhere else? Why?
Tell us about something new you have learnt recently. How did you learn it?
Do you think people will study more online in the future?
questions.explanation: Give your opinion and support it with reasons and examples from your own experience. Respond to what your partner says ('I agree with you, because...', 'I see what you mean, but...') and ask their opinion. Use present perfect for recent experiences ('I've just learnt to...'), comparatives for preferences ('It's easier to concentrate on my own') and will / might for the future.

questions.question: What is the girl going to buy for her brother's birthday?
options: a) a board game
b) a book about football
c) a football shirt
questions.explanation: The girl says she has 'gone for that new board game he keeps talking about'. She rejects the book because he has 'loads of those already', and the football shirt is what Dad has 'already bought him'.

questions.question: What time does the film start now?
options: a) quarter to seven
b) half past seven
c) quarter past six
questions.explanation: Tom says the cinema has changed the time: 'It's half past seven now'. Quarter to seven was the old time on the website, and quarter past six is when they will meet to eat.

questions.question: Where did the man find his phone?
options: a) at the gym
b) in the kitchen
c) in the car
questions.explanation: The man says 'it was under the passenger seat in the car'. He thought he had left it at the gym, but nobody had handed it in there, and he looked in the kitchen 'twice' without finding it.

questions.question: How will the woman get to work tomorrow?
options: a) by bus
b) by bike
c) on foot
questions.explanation: She says 'It's only forty minutes if I walk … so I'll just do that'. She can't cycle because of a flat tyre, and she decides against the bus because of the roadworks.

questions.question: What will Ben have for lunch?
options: a) pizza
b) a salad
c) pasta with tomato sauce
questions.explanation: When his dad suggests "the pasta with tomato sauce", Ben agrees and says he will have it. He had pizza the night before, and he does not want the salad because it comes with fish.

questions.question: Which sport has Amy just started?
options: a) tennis
b) basketball
c) swimming
questions.explanation: Amy says 'I've joined the tennis club near school … I've only had two lessons so far'. She gave up swimming last month, and basketball is her brother's sport, which she says is 'not for me'.

questions.question: What should the listener bring to the yoga class?
options: a) a notebook
b) a towel
c) a pair of trainers
questions.explanation: Karen says 'please bring your own towel, as we don't have enough for everyone'. Trainers are not needed because the class is done in bare feet, and a notebook is not necessary because she will email the exercises.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a camping trip. What does the woman say about it?
options: a) It cost more than she had planned.
b) The bad weather spoilt it.
c) It was better than she had expected.
questions.explanation: She wasn't keen before she went and 'thought I'd hate sleeping in a tent', but it 'turned out to be one of the best holidays I've ever had'. It rained only on the first night and did not spoil the trip, and she says it 'cost almost nothing'.

questions.question: You will hear two friends planning a trip to Edinburgh. What do they agree about?
options: a) They should go by train.
b) They should leave very early in the morning.
c) They should stay outside the city centre.
questions.explanation: After the man points out the problems with driving, the woman says 'on the train we could read or sleep' and 'Right, let's do that'. She refuses to catch the first train at five, and they do not agree about the hotel: the man says 'We can sort that out later'.

questions.question: You will hear a man talking about a hotel he stayed in. What did he like most about it?
options: a) Its position in the town
b) How quiet it was at night
c) The size of the rooms
questions.explanation: He says 'What I really liked was that it was right in the old town, so we could walk everywhere'. The rooms were 'a bit small', and although it was quiet at night, he mentions this only because he had expected noise; it is not what he liked most.

questions.question: You will hear a woman talking about a trip to Spain. Why is she going?
options: a) To spend time on the beach
b) To improve her Spanish
c) To visit members of her family
questions.explanation: She has booked a course because 'My Spanish is getting really rusty, and I'll need it for my new job'. Her cousins are coming to visit her instead, and she doubts she will have time for the beach.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about city breaks. What is the man's opinion of them?
options: a) They are too tiring.
b) They are too expensive.
c) They are too short.
questions.explanation: His problem is that 'by the time you've found your way around, it's time to go home', and he would rather go 'for a whole week'. He says they are 'not as expensive as people think' and that he doesn't mind all the walking.

questions.question: You will hear a woman phoning an airline. Why is she calling?
options: a) To complain about a delay
b) To change the date of her flight
c) To ask what she can take on the plane
questions.explanation: She asks 'Could you put me on a flight that day instead?' because she now needs to travel on the sixteenth, not the fourteenth. She says her call is not about today's delays, and she has already read the information about hand luggage.

questions.question: The group will fly to Barcelona from ____.
questions.explanation: Mrs Hughes says 'We'll be flying from Manchester, not Liverpool as I said in my first letter'. Liverpool was the airport in the first letter, so it is no longer correct.

questions.question: In Barcelona, the students will stay in a ____ near the beach.
questions.explanation: She says 'we'll be staying in a youth hostel near the beach'.

questions.question: Students will need extra money to pay for their ____.
questions.explanation: Breakfast and dinner are included, 'but you'll have to buy your own lunch, so bring some extra money for that'.

questions.question: On Thursday morning, students will have lessons at a local ____ school.
questions.explanation: She says they will 'spend the morning at a local secondary school, where you'll have lessons with Spanish students'. The word needed before 'school' is 'secondary'.

questions.question: Because the football stadium is closed, the group will visit the ____ instead.
questions.explanation: The football stadium is 'closed for building work', 'so instead we'll go to the science museum'.

questions.question: Because the weather can change, students should pack a ____ jacket.
questions.explanation: She says 'the weather in April can be quite changeable, so bring a waterproof jacket as well as sun cream'.

questions.question: How did Hannah feel when she first worked in a kitchen?
options: a) Surprised by how hard the work was
b) Bored by the simple tasks she had to do
c) Sure that she had chosen the right job
questions.explanation: She thought she knew what to expect, 'but I was shocked. The heat, the noise, twelve hours on your feet'. She 'wasn't sure I'd last', so she was not sure about the job, and she says she 'didn't mind the washing-up itself', so she was not bored.

questions.question: What does Hannah say was most useful about catering college?
options: a) She learnt most of her cooking skills there.
b) It helped her with the written work.
c) She met people who helped her find work.
questions.explanation: She says 'What really mattered was that my tutors knew everyone in the business', and one of them introduced her to the chef who gave her her first job. She learnt most of her skills 'in real kitchens', not at college, and the written work was already easy for her.

questions.question: What is Hannah's opinion of cooking competitions on TV?
options: a) She would like to take part in one, as her mum suggests.
b) They are fun to watch with her family.
c) They give the wrong idea of what chefs do.
questions.explanation: She says 'they make it look as if being a chef is all about exciting moments and big prizes', while real work is 'cooking the same dishes perfectly, night after night'. She says 'I'd never do it', and it is her mum who loves them; she doesn't really watch them herself.

questions.question: Why did Hannah open her own restaurant?
options: a) She wanted to use food from her local area.
b) She hoped to earn more money than before.
c) She did not get on with her last boss very well.
questions.explanation: 'The real reason was that I wanted to cook with ingredients from the farms around here, where I grew up.' She earns less now than before, and she says her last boss 'was brilliant'.

questions.question: How does Hannah feel about being a young head chef?
options: a) Worried that she does not have enough experience.
b) Annoyed that some people don't see her as the chef.
c) Sure that her age makes her a better cook.
questions.explanation: Suppliers 'ask to speak to the chef when I'm standing right in front of them, and that still annoys me'. She says being young doesn't make her 'better or worse at cooking', and with eight years in kitchens 'experience isn't really the issue'.

questions.question: What advice does Hannah give to young people who want to be chefs?
options: a) Go to catering college as soon as possible.
b) Get some experience in a real kitchen first.
c) Learn to cook as many kinds of food as possible.
questions.explanation: She says 'Get a part-time job in a real kitchen first … and see if you can cope with it'. She tells them not to sign up for a course straight away, and not to try to learn every kind of food.

questions.question: Marco is going on holiday to Spain next summer. He has never studied Spanish before. He wants to be able to talk to people while he is there and isn't interested in learning to write.
options: A) World Kitchen
B) Breads of the World
C) Spanish for Travellers
D) Spanish at Work
E) Photography Made Simple
F) Guitar for Beginners
G) Watercolour Painting
H) Story Writing Workshop
questions.explanation: Spanish for Travellers is 'for complete beginners', 'concentrates on speaking' and has 'very little grammar or writing'. Spanish at Work also teaches Spanish, but it is for students who 'already have some knowledge of Spanish' and focuses on writing emails and reports.

questions.question: Hannah wants to learn how to take better photos. She doesn't own a camera, only a mobile phone. She would also like the course to include some time outside.
options: A) World Kitchen
B) Breads of the World
C) Spanish for Travellers
D) Spanish at Work
E) Photography Made Simple
F) Guitar for Beginners
G) Watercolour Painting
H) Story Writing Workshop
questions.explanation: Photography Made Simple says 'a mobile phone is perfectly fine' and 'includes two Saturday walks in the countryside'. Watercolour Painting also has lessons outdoors in the park, but it teaches painting, not photography.

questions.question: Sofia would like to learn how to make food from different countries. She finishes work at seven o'clock, so her class cannot start before half past seven. She wants to take what she makes home for her husband to try.
options: A) World Kitchen
B) Breads of the World
C) Spanish for Travellers
D) Spanish at Work
E) Photography Made Simple
F) Guitar for Beginners
G) Watercolour Painting
H) Story Writing Workshop
questions.explanation: Breads of the World teaches 'breads from around the world', starts at 8 p.m. and 'you can take everything you bake home to share with your family'. World Kitchen also teaches food from other countries, but it starts at 6 p.m. and the group eats the meal together at the end of the class.

questions.question: Laura enjoys writing stories in her free time. She would like other people to give her advice on her writing, and she hopes that the public will be able to read her work.
options: A) World Kitchen
B) Breads of the World
C) Spanish for Travellers
D) Spanish at Work
E) Photography Made Simple
F) Guitar for Beginners
G) Watercolour Painting
H) Story Writing Workshop
questions.explanation: In the Story Writing Workshop students read their work to the group, 'who will give you friendly advice', and 'the best stories are published in the college's online magazine'. Spanish at Work also involves writing, but only work emails and reports, not stories.

questions.question: Oliver has always wanted to play a musical instrument, but he hasn't got one. He'd prefer to learn in a small group, where the teacher has time for every student.
options: A) World Kitchen
B) Breads of the World
C) Spanish for Travellers
D) Spanish at Work
E) Photography Made Simple
F) Guitar for Beginners
G) Watercolour Painting
H) Story Writing Workshop
questions.explanation: Guitar for Beginners says 'Guitars are provided' and classes have 'a maximum of six students, which means the teacher can help everyone'. The Story Writing Workshop also has small groups, but it does not teach a musical instrument.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.
questions.explanation: The writer has just said they had no experience and 'weren't particularly fit'; 'In fact' explains that they did not choose the trip because they loved cycling, and the next sentence gives the real reason: 'We simply thought it would be a cheap and healthy way to see a beautiful part of the country'. The sentence about Clare having cycled the route before cannot fit, because the text says 'Neither of us had any experience'.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.
questions.explanation: 'This' refers to Pete showing them 'how to fix a flat tyre', and 'we were glad of it later' prepares for the flat tyre on the third morning. The sentence about repairing the tyre cannot go here, because nothing has broken yet.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.
questions.explanation: The road 'goes up and down constantly' and their legs were aching, so they had to push their bikes up 'the steepest hills'. The next sentence continues the idea: 'the views of the sea from the top of each hill made all the effort worthwhile'. Taking the train cannot fit, as they cycled all the way to Penzance.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.
questions.explanation: There was 'no bike shop for miles', but 'however' shows a contrast: because Pete had taught them, they could 'repair it' (the flat tyre) themselves, and 'Twenty minutes later we were back on our bikes'. Camping in a field cannot fit, because they continued cycling and stayed in guest houses.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (5)?
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.
questions.explanation: 'The owners' are the owners of the guest houses mentioned just before, and the next sentence, 'Most of them were also happy to let us keep our bikes…', continues describing them. Camping in a field contradicts the guest houses they had booked.

questions.question: Gap (1): More than eighty volunteers took part ____ our town's first beach clean-up day.
questions.explanation: 'Take part in something' is a fixed expression meaning 'join an activity'. 'Part' is always followed by 'in' before the event.

questions.question: Gap (2): You wouldn't expect to find a fridge on a beach, ____ you?
questions.explanation: This is a question tag. The main sentence uses 'wouldn't', so the positive tag repeats the same modal: 'would you?'. 'Do you' or 'will you' do not match 'wouldn't'.

questions.question: Gap (3): We counted how ____ bottles we collected: over six hundred.
questions.explanation: 'Bottles' is a plural countable noun, so we ask about quantity with 'how many'. 'How much' is used with uncountable nouns, and 'how few' does not fit 'over six hundred'.

questions.question: Gap (4): The council had to send a second one to take it all ____.
questions.explanation: 'Too much ... for' means more than something can hold: the rubbish did not fit in one lorry, so the council had to send a second one.

questions.question: Gap (5): I found ____ hard to believe how dirty the beach was.
questions.explanation: In 'find + it + adjective + to-infinitive', 'it' is an empty object that stands for the idea that follows ('to believe how dirty the beach was'). Without 'it' the sentence is not correct.

questions.question: Gap (6): The students now hope to hold a clean-up every spring, ____ or not the council helps them again.
questions.explanation: 'Whether or not' means 'it does not matter if'. The students will do it in any case. 'If' is not possible directly before 'or not'.

questions.question:
You must answer this question. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Read this email from your English-speaking friend, Alex, and the notes you have made.

From: Alex
Subject: Guess what!

Hi!

I've got some great news: I've found a flat to rent, and it's in your neighbourhood! I'm moving in at the end of next month. (Note 1: Great!)

I don't know the area at all yet. What's the best thing about living there? (Note 2: Tell Alex)

I'll need to do a lot of shopping for the flat. Where do you think I should go? (Note 3: Suggest…)

And would you like to help me on moving day? I'll buy you lunch! (Note 4: Yes, but…)

See you soon,
Alex

Write your email to Alex using all the notes.
questions.explanation: A good answer is an informal email of about 100 words that covers all four notes: reacts with pleasure to Alex's news (Great!), describes the best thing about the neighbourhood with a reason (Tell Alex), suggests a place to shop for the flat and says why (Suggest…), and agrees to help on moving day while adding a condition or problem, for example a time when you are busy (Yes, but…). It should open and close like an email to a friend and use linking words such as because, so and but.

questions.question:
Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question A: Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for teenagers.

Articles wanted!
My ideal home
Where would your ideal home be? What would it look like, and what would you have in it? Why would it be perfect for you?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Question B: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
The old house at the end of the street was finally sold.

Write your story.
questions.explanation: Article: a good answer has an interesting title, speaks directly to the reader, and answers all the questions in the notice: where the ideal home would be, what it would look like and contain, and why it would be perfect, using the second conditional (it would have…, I would…). Story: a good answer begins with the given sentence, has a clear sequence of events and a satisfying ending, and uses past tenses and time linkers (at first, then, suddenly, in the end). Both answers should be about 100 words.

questions.question:
Answer the examiner's questions about yourself. Give full answers, with reasons or examples.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. What do you usually have for breakfast?
3. Who does most of the cooking in your home?
4. What's your favourite meal of the day? Why?
5. Tell us about a meal you really enjoyed recently.
6. Do you prefer eating at home or eating out? Why?
questions.explanation: A good answer goes beyond one word: for example, 'I usually just have toast and a cup of tea, because I don't have much time before school.' The candidate should use present simple for habits, past simple for the recent meal, and give a reason with because or so for the opinion questions.

questions.question: Look at the photograph. It shows a family sharing a meal together at home. Tell us what you can see in the photograph. Talk about the people, the food, the place and what you think is happening. You have about one minute.
questions.explanation: A good answer describes the people (how many, their ages, what they are wearing and doing), the food and drink on the table, and the room, using the present continuous (they are passing a plate, a girl is laughing) and place expressions (in the middle, on the left, in the background). It also guesses about the situation with phrases such as 'It looks like…' or 'Maybe they are celebrating…', and uses paraphrase when the candidate does not know a word.

questions.question:
Talk together with your partner. Your class wants to have a meal together to celebrate the end of the school year. Here are some ideas for the meal:

a barbecue in the park
a meal at a pizza restaurant
everyone cooks a dish at home and brings it to school
a picnic on the beach
cooking a meal together in the school kitchen

Talk together about the different ideas and say which would be most enjoyable for the class. Then decide which idea is best.
questions.explanation: A good answer discusses several of the ideas with advantages and disadvantages (cost, weather, how much work it is, whether everyone can take part), asks for the partner's opinion ('What do you think?', 'Do you agree?'), agrees and disagrees politely ('That's a good idea, but…'), makes suggestions with 'Why don't we…' or 'How about…', and finishes by reaching a decision together.

questions.question:
Discuss these questions with your partner and the examiner:

1. Do you enjoy cooking? What can you cook?
2. Do you think young people should learn to cook at school? Why or why not?
3. What kinds of restaurants are popular in your town?
4. Is it better to eat with your family or with friends? Why?
5. Do people eat more fast food now than in the past? Why do you think this is?
questions.explanation: A good answer gives opinions with reasons and examples from personal experience, reacts to what the partner says ('I agree with you because…', 'I see what you mean, but…'), and uses a range of tenses, for example present perfect for experience (I've never cooked…) and comparisons between now and the past.

questions.question: What should guests do if they need breakfast before 7.00?
options: a) Go to reception at 10 p.m. to have something to eat.
b) Collect a packed breakfast from the restaurant at 5.30.
c) Ask at reception for a packed breakfast the evening before.
questions.explanation: The notice says 'please order a packed breakfast at reception before 10 pm the night before'. The breakfast is collected from reception, not from the restaurant, and 10 pm is the latest time to order, not a time to eat.

questions.question: What does Mia want Sam to do?
options: a) Tell her whether she should book the Sunday trip.
b) Go to the tourist office before 5 o'clock.
c) Change their train tickets to a later time on Sunday.
questions.explanation: Mia asks 'Do you want me to book them and change the train, or shall we forget the trip? Let me know by 5.' She wants Sam's decision. She offers to change the train herself, so Sam does not have to do it, and nobody needs to go to the office by 5 – that is only when she needs an answer.

questions.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) Children are not allowed in the pool on Thursday.
b) The gym is closed on Thursday morning.
c) Young children cannot swim without an adult.
questions.explanation: The sign says 'Children under 12 must be with an adult at all times.' On Thursday morning the pool is closed for everyone, not only children, and it is open again later; the gym 'will stay open as usual'.

questions.question: What does the notice say about the walking tours?
options: a) Visitors have to pay the guide at the end.
b) Large groups should arrange their tour beforehand.
c) Everyone must book a place at the office the day before.
questions.explanation: 'Groups of more than ten people, please contact us in advance' means big groups should arrange it beforehand. The notice says 'There is no need to book – just turn up', and the tours are free: tips are welcome but not required.

questions.question: Why has the hotel written to Mr Price?
options: a) To ask him to agree to a change for one night.
b) To offer him a cheaper room for his whole stay.
c) To tell him that his booking has been cancelled.
questions.explanation: The sea-view room is 'not available on your first night', so the hotel offers another room that night and asks him to 'let us know if this is acceptable'. The change is only for the first night, the price stays the same ('at no extra cost'), and the booking is not cancelled.

questions.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) The sales team must write their names on the door of the room.
b) Anyone can use this room on Tuesday mornings if it is empty.
c) People who want the room at other times should book it at reception.
questions.explanation: The notice says 'If you need it at any other time, please write your name and the time on the list at reception'. The room is booked for the sales team on Tuesday mornings, so it is not free for anyone then, and names should go on the reception list, 'not on this door'.

questions.question: Why has Priya written to Tom?
options: a) To warn him that colour printing is no longer possible in the office
b) To tell him where he can print until the printer is repaired
c) To ask him to contact the engineer before Thursday
questions.explanation: Priya writes 'Until then, please use the one on the second floor', so she is telling Tom which printer to use until the engineer comes. She does not ask him to contact the engineer, and she only says the second-floor printer is black and white, not that colour printing is impossible for good.

questions.question: What should staff do?
options: a) Stay out of the kitchen while the fridge is being cleaned.
b) Clean the fridge themselves on Friday at 4 p.m.
c) Put a name label on any food they want to keep.
questions.explanation: The notice says food 'without a name on it will be thrown away' and 'items with a name label can stay', so staff should label food they want to keep. The kitchen is not closed, and the notice says the fridge 'will be cleaned', not that staff must clean it.

questions.question: How will staff get the new Wi-Fi password?
options: a) They will be sent it in a text message.
b) They can collect it from reception on Monday.
c) They have to choose a new one before Monday.
questions.explanation: Maria writes 'Everyone will receive the new password by text message early on Monday morning'. She says reception 'won't have it', and staff do not choose the password themselves.

questions.question: What does Jack need to do?
options: a) Phone Mr Evans to confirm the new meeting time
b) Tell Mr Evans that the meeting will start later this afternoon
c) Wait for Mr Evans to phone again later today
questions.explanation: Sam writes 'Could you call him back to confirm?' after explaining that Mr Evans wants to move the meeting to tomorrow at the same time. So Jack must phone Mr Evans; he is not asked to wait for another call, and the meeting is moving to tomorrow, not starting later today.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (1).
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.
questions.explanation: 'Learning in this way' refers back to learning 'at their kitchen table, on the bus or even in bed', and the idea that it 'has become completely normal' is supported by the next sentence: 'more than half of all adults have now taken at least one course on the internet'. The sentence about printed textbooks is about paper books, so it breaks the link between these two sentences.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (2).
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.
questions.explanation: The paragraph begins 'There are several reasons for this growth. The most obvious is ...', so 'Another reason' continues the list. The idea that students 'decide for themselves when to study' is then explained by the example of the nurse who 'can study during the day' and the parent who waits 'until the children are asleep'. The sentence saying courses 'cost more' contradicts 'faster and cheaper', and the one about schools needing fewer teachers is not what the nurse example shows.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (3).
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.
questions.explanation: 'Some go even further' refers to the universities that put 'recordings of their lectures on the internet', and adds a bigger step: 'complete courses that anyone can join for free'. The next sentence, 'Some of these have attracted over a million students', needs these free courses as its subject. Printed textbooks do not attract 'students' in a lecture hall, so that sentence cannot fit.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (4).
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.
questions.explanation: 'The main reason' explains why many people 'never finish' their course, and 'a lack of motivation' is then described in the next sentence: without a teacher, 'they find it easy to put off the next lesson'. The sentence about schools employing fewer teachers does not explain why people stop studying.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (5).
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.
questions.explanation: 'These' refers to the 'ways for learners to stay in touch with each other', and the sentence gives examples: 'discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners'. The following sentence about students who 'feel part of a group' continues this idea. The sentence about online courses costing more has no link to staying in touch.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.
questions.explanation: The sentence before says 'It is easy to think that teenagers are simply lazy.' 'However' contrasts with this idea, and 'a much better explanation' introduces the next paragraph, which explains the body clock. The sentence about online time cannot go here because phones have not been mentioned yet.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.
questions.explanation: 'In other words' repeats the idea that melatonin arrives 'two hours later' in simpler words. The next sentence, 'But school still starts at the same time', contrasts with 'not ready for sleep until much later', and 'their bodies' is repeated in 'before their bodies are ready to wake up'. The sentence saying teenagers 'sleep much longer' contradicts the article.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.
questions.explanation: 'The difference' refers to 'between eight and ten hours' needed and 'fewer than seven' actually slept. 'A serious effect' is then explained by the list that follows: students find it harder to concentrate, feel anxious and catch colds. The sentence saying teachers 'did not notice any difference' contradicts these effects.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.
questions.explanation: The sentence before describes teenagers who 'message friends or watch videos until late' – the time they spend online. The gap sentence says this is not the only problem, and the next sentence gives the second problem with 'also': 'The light from the screen also tells the brain that it is still daytime.' The sentence about morning light cannot go here because 'help too' needs an earlier piece of advice.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (5)?
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.
questions.explanation: The sentence before gives two pieces of advice from sleep experts, and 'can help too' adds a third. The next sentence, 'Some schools ... have even started lessons an hour later', adds one more solution. The sentence saying 'none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement' cannot go here: it refers to 'this' before the later start has been mentioned, and it contradicts the teachers, who say students 'get better marks'.

questions.question: Why did Maya decide to create the app?
options: a) Her grandmother had asked the neighbours for help and they had refused.
b) She wanted to enter a competition for young app designers.
c) Her parents asked her to find a way of looking after her grandmother.
d) Her grandmother's neighbours wanted to help but did not know when.
questions.explanation: Maya says the neighbours 'would happily help' but 'they never knew when she actually needed something'. Her grandmother did not ask for help at all – she was 'too proud to knock on their doors and ask' – so the neighbours never refused her.

questions.question: What does Maya say about the first version of Next Door?
options: a) It stopped working as soon as a few people used it together.
b) It took her only a few weeks to build from online videos.
c) She built it with help from her teacher.
d) Her parents helped her to test it at weekends.
questions.explanation: Maya says 'It crashed every time more than two people used it at once'. She spent six months teaching herself, not a few weeks, and her teacher only helped her later, after he noticed her working on the app at lunch.

questions.question: How did Mr Okafor help Maya?
options: a) He recommended some free online videos to her.
b) He let her work on the app during his lessons.
c) He asked her questions until she saw her own mistakes.
d) He corrected the problems in her code himself at lunch.
questions.explanation: Maya says 'He didn't fix it for me. He just asked the right questions until I understood what I'd done wrong.' She found the online videos herself, and he saw her working on the app during a lunch break, not in lessons.

questions.question: Why has Maya refused to sell the app?
options: a) The companies did not offer her enough money.
b) She wants it to stay free for people who might not be able to pay.
c) She is worried that selling it would take up too much of her time.
d) She is planning to charge users for it herself.
questions.explanation: The companies 'wanted to add advertising and charge people to use it', and Maya says 'The people who need it most are often the ones with the least money'. She does not mention the amount of money offered, and she does not want anyone to pay.

questions.question: What advice does Maya give to young people with an idea?
options: a) Ask an expert to check your idea before you do anything.
b) Try hard to avoid making mistakes in the early stages.
c) Start small and accept that things will go wrong.
d) Wait until you have all the skills you need before starting.
questions.explanation: Maya says 'Start with something small, and expect it to go wrong. That's how you learn.' She also says 'Don't wait until you feel ready', which is the opposite of waiting until you have all the skills, and she sees mistakes as the way to learn rather than something to avoid.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
options: a) get
b) do
c) take
d) make
questions.explanation: The fixed collocation is 'make changes' ('the secret is to make small changes'). We do not say 'do changes', 'take changes' or 'get changes' in English.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
options: a) skipping
b) passing
c) dropping
d) jumping
questions.explanation: To 'skip breakfast' means not to eat it, which matches 'because you are in a hurry'. 'Passing', 'dropping' and 'jumping' are not used with a meal to mean not eating it.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
options: a) remain
b) keep
c) stay
d) hold
questions.explanation: The pattern is 'keep somebody + adjective': porridge 'will keep you full of energy'. 'Stay' and 'remain' cannot take an object ('you'), and 'hold you full of energy' is not possible.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
options: a) make
b) pay
c) put
d) take
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'pay attention to' something: 'pay attention to how much sugar there is'. 'Make', 'put' and 'take' do not go with 'attention' in this way.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
options: a) advertised
b) informed
c) announced
d) noticed
questions.explanation: Products are 'advertised as healthy' when companies sell them with this message, which contrasts with 'actually contain a surprising amount' of sugar. We cannot say a product is 'informed', 'announced' or 'noticed as healthy'.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
options: a) caring
b) paying
c) noticing
d) looking
questions.explanation: 'Without noticing it' means without realising what is happening: when your mind is on something else, you eat too much and don't notice. 'Looking it' and 'caring it' are not grammatical (we say 'look at' and 'care about'), and 'paying it' makes no sense here.

passages.title: New Library Services
passages.text: Hello everyone. I am here to tell you about the exciting changes coming to our local library next month. First, we are introducing a new online reservation system. You will be able to book books from home using your library card number. We are also opening a new study area on the second floor, which will be equipped with ten high-speed computers. For those who enjoy reading outside, we are launching a 'Books in the Park' scheme where you can borrow items from a mobile stand near the fountain. Please note that the library will be closed for renovations on the 15th of July. If you need help with your digital skills, we are starting free weekly workshops every Wednesday morning. Finally, if you have any suggestions, please leave a note in the suggestion box located next to the main entrance.

passages.title: School Trip to France
passages.text: Hello everyone. I am here to give you the final details about our upcoming school trip to France. We will be departing from the school gates at 7:30 am on Monday morning, so please make sure you arrive on time. We are staying at a lovely hotel in the countryside, which is famous for its large swimming pool. On the first day, we will visit a local museum to learn about history. The most exciting part of the trip will be the visit to the chocolate factory on Wednesday, where we can taste everything! For lunch, we will have a picnic in the park, but please remember to bring a bottle of water. Finally, don't forget to bring your camera to take photos of the beautiful scenery. I am sure we will have a fantastic time!

passages.title: New Sports Centre Opening
passages.text: Hello everyone! I am delighted to announce that the Riverside Sports Centre will finally open its doors to the public next Monday. We have spent months preparing the facilities. If you are interested in swimming, our main pool is 25 metres long and has a special area for children. For those who prefer fitness, the gym is equipped with the latest machines, and we offer a variety of classes including yoga and aerobics. We are currently looking for a receptionist to join our team, so please check our website if you are interested. Membership fees are very reasonable, and if you sign up before the end of the month, you will receive a discount of 15 percent on your first year. We also have a cafe on the ground floor where you can relax after your workout. We look forward to seeing you there!

passages.title: Interview with a Game Designer
passages.text: Interviewer: Today we are talking to Sarah Jenkins, who designs video games for a living. Sarah, was it always your dream to work in this industry? Sarah: Actually, no. I studied architecture at university. I loved drawing buildings, but I found the work a bit slow. One day, a friend showed me how to code a simple game, and I was hooked. I realized that game design is like architecture, but you can build entire worlds that people can interact with. Interviewer: That sounds fascinating. What is the most challenging part of your job? Sarah: People think it is just playing games all day, but it is actually very stressful. We have strict deadlines. If the game isn't ready for the holiday season, the company loses a lot of money. Sometimes I spend 12 hours a day staring at code. Interviewer: Do you ever get tired of it? Sarah: Sometimes, but then I see someone playing a game I helped create, and their face lights up. That feeling is worth all the hard work. Interviewer: What advice would you give to young people wanting to enter the field? Sarah: Don't just play games—learn how they are made. Start with simple tools and don't be afraid to make mistakes. Your first game will probably be terrible, and that is perfectly fine!

passages.title: Interview with Travel Blogger Sarah Jenkins
passages.text: Interviewer: Sarah, you've been blogging for five years now. What made you start? Sarah: I was working in an office and felt bored. I took a trip to Peru and realized I wanted to share my experiences. Interviewer: Was it hard to get started? Sarah: Yes, I didn't know anything about photography or writing for an audience. I had to learn everything from scratch. Interviewer: Many people think travel blogging is just a holiday. What do you say to them? Sarah: It's definitely not! I spend hours editing photos and researching locations. It's a full-time job. Interviewer: Do you ever get lonely? Sarah: Sometimes, but I meet so many interesting people on the road that it balances out. Interviewer: What is your favorite part of the job? Sarah: Seeing a place I've only read about in books. It's magical. Interviewer: Any advice for beginners? Sarah: Be yourself. Don't try to copy other bloggers. Authenticity is what people want to see.

passages.title: Interview with a young chef
passages.text: Interviewer: Today we are joined by Maya, a 22-year-old chef who recently opened her first restaurant. Maya, was it always your dream to cook professionally? Maya: Honestly, no. I studied graphic design first! But I spent all my free time helping my grandmother in her kitchen. I realized that the pressure of a busy service was actually where I felt most alive. Interviewer: Many people find the long hours in a kitchen difficult. How do you manage? Maya: It is exhausting, I won't lie. You are on your feet for twelve hours. But I have a great team, and we support each other. If I didn't love the creativity of inventing new dishes, I would have quit months ago. Interviewer: What is the most challenging part of your job? Maya: People think it's the cooking, but it's actually the management. Ordering ingredients, dealing with staff, and keeping the budget in check—that's the real work. The cooking is the reward at the end of the day. Interviewer: Do you have advice for young people wanting to enter the industry? Maya: Don't expect to be a head chef immediately. Start at the bottom, learn how to clean, how to prep, and be humble. You need to be willing to fail a few times before you get it right.

passages.title: Interview with a young chef
passages.text: Interviewer: Today we are talking to Sarah Jenkins, who recently opened her own restaurant at just twenty-two. Sarah, was it always your dream to be a chef? Sarah: Actually, no. I wanted to be a musician, but I loved cooking for friends. Then, I took a summer job in a kitchen and realized I preferred the heat of the stove to the stage! Interviewer: Was it difficult to start your own business so young? Sarah: The hardest part wasn't the cooking, but the paperwork. I spent weeks talking to banks and finding the right location. I almost gave up once, but my mentor encouraged me to keep going. Interviewer: What is the most popular dish on your menu? Sarah: Definitely the spicy vegetable stew. I thought people would find it too hot, but they love it. I use a secret spice mix from my grandmother. Interviewer: What do you do when you are not working? Sarah: I try to get away from food entirely! I go hiking or read books. If I stay in the kitchen too long, I lose my creativity. Interviewer: What advice would you give to other young people? Sarah: Don't be afraid to make mistakes. Every burnt meal is a lesson.

passages.title: A New Beginning
passages.text:
Moving to a new city is often described as an exciting adventure, but for me, it felt more like a challenge I wasn't ready for. Last summer, my parents announced that we were moving from our quiet village to the bustling city of Manchester. I had lived in the same house for fourteen years, and the thought of leaving my friends and my favourite local park was devastating.

When we first arrived, the noise was the biggest shock. Unlike the peaceful nights I was used to, the city never seemed to sleep. There were sirens, traffic, and people talking at all hours. For the first two weeks, I barely left my room. I felt like an outsider looking in, convinced that I would never fit into this fast-paced environment. I spent most of my time messaging my old friends, feeling sorry for myself.

However, everything changed when I joined a local photography club. I had always enjoyed taking pictures, and I thought it might be a good way to get out of the house. On my first day, I met a girl named Sarah who was also new to the area. We started exploring the city together, looking for interesting buildings and street art to photograph. Through her eyes, I began to see the city differently. Instead of just seeing traffic and noise, I started to notice the beautiful architecture and the vibrant culture.

It has been six months now, and I can honestly say I don't regret the move. While I still miss my old friends, I have built a new life here. I have learned that moving isn't just about changing your address; it is about changing your perspective. You have to be willing to step outside your comfort zone to find the hidden gems in any new place. If you are facing a big move, my advice is to find a hobby or a group that shares your interests. It makes the world feel a lot smaller and much friendlier.

passages.title: A Life-Changing Summer in Peru
passages.text: Last summer, I decided to do something completely different. Instead of spending my holidays at home, I signed up for a volunteer program in a small village in the Peruvian Andes. I had always wanted to travel, but I wanted to do more than just visit tourist sites; I wanted to make a real difference. When I arrived, I was surprised by how different everything was. The air was thin, the mountains were breathtaking, and the local community was incredibly welcoming. My main job was to help build a new classroom for the primary school. I had never held a hammer or painted a wall before, but the local builders were very patient with me. They taught me how to mix cement and how to work as part of a team. It was hard physical work, especially in the heat, but I felt a great sense of achievement every evening. In the afternoons, I helped the children with their English homework. They were so eager to learn, and we often spent hours laughing as we tried to communicate through gestures and simple words. Living without electricity and limited internet access was a challenge at first. I missed my friends and the comforts of home, but as the weeks passed, I realized that I didn't need those things to be happy. I learned to appreciate the simple things, like a shared meal or a beautiful sunset over the peaks. This experience changed my perspective on life. I realized that we don't need much to be happy, and that helping others is one of the most rewarding things you can do. I returned home with a new sense of purpose and a promise to myself that I would continue volunteering in the future. I have already started looking for local opportunities in my own city.

passages.title: Rising Star: An Interview with Leo Vance

At just sixteen, Leo Vance has already made a name for himself in the world of competitive swimming. We caught up with him at his local training centre in Manchester. 'I started swimming when I was five,' Leo explains, drying off after a two-hour morning session. 'My parents took me to the pool every weekend, but I didn't really take it seriously until I joined a club at ten.'

Leo’s routine is demanding. He wakes up at 4:30 a.m. to be in the water by 5:15 a.m. 'It’s tough, especially in winter when it's dark and cold outside,' he admits. 'But when you’re in the pool, you forget the time. You just focus on your strokes.' Despite the hard work, Leo insists he has a normal social life. 'People think athletes don't have time for friends, but I make sure I see my mates on Friday nights. It’s important to switch off.'

His biggest challenge so far was the National Youth Championships last year. 'I was so nervous before the final race,' he recalls. 'I almost pulled out, but my coach reminded me why I started. I ended up winning silver.' That medal changed his perspective. 'It wasn't just about the prize; it was about proving to myself that I could handle the pressure.'

Looking ahead, Leo has his sights set on the international stage. 'The dream is the Olympics, obviously. But for now, I’m focused on improving my technique. My coach says I’m strong, but my turns need work.' When asked if he has any advice for other young athletes, he is humble. 'Don't let the sport define who you are. Enjoy it, work hard, but remember to have fun. If you stop enjoying it, you’ll never reach your potential.'

passages.title: Interview with a Travel Blogger
passages.text:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Elena Rossi, a successful travel blogger. Elena, welcome. Why did you first start your blog, 'Elena's Footsteps'?

Elena: Well, I didn't plan to make it my job! I actually started it when I went on a gap year to South America. My parents were really worried, so I promised to write regular updates so they'd know I was safe. I didn't think anyone else would read it, but then other travelers started finding my posts and asking for advice.

Interviewer: That's amazing. You've been to so many countries. Which one stands out the most?

Elena: People always ask this! I love Japan for its food, and Iceland for the landscapes, but my absolute favorite was Albania. I didn't know much about it before going, but the local people were incredibly welcoming. One family even invited me into their home for dinner when I got lost. That kindness is what I remember most.

Interviewer: Traveling isn't always easy, though. How do you deal with things when they go wrong?

Elena: Oh, I've had missed flights, lost luggage, and food poisoning! At first, I used to get really stressed and angry. But I quickly realized that doesn't help. Now, I just accept that problems are part of the adventure. I try to stay calm and look for a solution, often by asking locals. They are usually happy to help a confused tourist.

Interviewer: You usually travel by yourself. Do you prefer that?

Elena: I do. When you travel with friends, you tend to stay in your own little bubble. But when you're on your own, you're forced to talk to strangers, which means you make new friends much faster. Of course, it can be lonely occasionally, but the freedom to decide where to go next without arguing is worth it.

Interviewer: What's the most challenging part of being a professional blogger?

Elena: People think it's a permanent holiday, but it's hard work. The toughest thing for me is the lack of a routine. I'm constantly moving, which makes it hard to exercise regularly or eat healthily. I don't mind the long hours spent editing photos or writing posts, because I love doing that, but not having a proper home base can be exhausting.

Interviewer: Finally, what tips do you have for someone wanting to start a travel blog?

Elena: Don't just write about the famous tourist spots that everyone knows. Try to find a unique angle. Write about your personal feelings and the small details, like the smell of a local market. And most importantly, write because you love it, not because you want to get free hotel rooms. Readers can tell if you aren't being genuine.
