Sam

passages.title: The rise of online learning
passages.text:
Twenty years ago, learning a new language or studying for a qualification usually meant sitting in a classroom at a fixed time each week. Today, millions of people learn at their kitchen table, on the bus or even in bed. (1) ______ In some countries, more than half of all adults have now taken at least one course on the internet.

There are several reasons for this growth. The most obvious is that the internet has become faster and cheaper, so watching video lessons is no longer a problem for most people. (2) ______ For example, a nurse who works nights can study during the day, while a parent can wait until the children are asleep.

Universities have also played a part. Many of them now put recordings of their lectures on the internet. (3) ______ Some of these have attracted over a million students, which would be impossible in any lecture hall.

However, online learning is not perfect. Many people sign up for a course with great enthusiasm but never finish it. (4) ______ Without a teacher checking their progress, they find it easy to put off the next lesson until tomorrow, and then the day after.

To solve this problem, many course designers now include ways for learners to stay in touch with each other. (5) ______ Students who feel part of a group, it seems, are much more likely to reach the end. In the future, the best courses may combine the freedom of learning online with the support that classrooms have always provided.

passages.title: Why teenagers need their sleep
passages.text:
Most parents have had the same experience. They knock on their teenager's bedroom door at nine o'clock on a Saturday morning. There is no answer. It is easy to think that teenagers are simply lazy. (1) ______

During the teenage years, the body's internal 'clock' changes. This clock controls our daily pattern of sleeping and waking. The brain starts producing melatonin, the chemical that makes us feel sleepy, around two hours later than it did in childhood. (2) ______ But school still starts at the same time, so the alarm goes off long before their bodies are ready to wake up.

Sleep matters at every age, but it is especially important for teenagers. Experts say teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night. Surveys show that most of them get fewer than seven. (3) ______ Students who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate in class and to remember what they have learnt. They are also more likely to feel anxious or low. They catch colds more often, too. Their results in sport can suffer as well.

Phones make the problem worse. Many teenagers take them to bed and message friends or watch videos until late. (4) ______ The light from the screen also tells the brain that it is still daytime, so melatonin arrives even later.

So what can teenagers do? There are some simple answers. Sleep experts suggest going to bed at the same time every night, even at weekends, and leaving phones in another room. (5) ______ Some schools in the UK and the USA have even started lessons an hour later, and teachers there say that students are more awake and get better marks. Perhaps other schools will soon follow their example.

passages.title: The teenager who helped a whole street
passages.text:
When sixteen-year-old Maya Collins started building an app in her bedroom two years ago, she had no idea that it would soon be used by more than fifty thousand people. 'Honestly, I just wanted to solve a problem in my own family,' she says.

The problem began one winter. Maya's grandmother slipped on some ice and broke her leg. She lived alone, and although Maya's parents visited as often as they could, they both worked long hours in another town. 'Gran's neighbours kept telling us they would happily help her with shopping or collecting medicine,' Maya explains. 'But they never knew when she actually needed something, and she was too proud to knock on their doors and ask.'

That gave Maya the idea for Next Door, an app which lets older people post small requests that neighbours nearby can accept with one click. There was only one difficulty: Maya had never written a line of computer code. She spent the next six months teaching herself from free online videos, often working until midnight at weekends. 'My first version was a disaster,' she laughs. 'It crashed every time more than two people used it at once.'

Help came from an unexpected place. Maya's computer science teacher, Mr Okafor, noticed her working on the app during a lunch break and offered to look at it with her. 'He didn't fix it for me,' she says. 'He just asked the right questions until I understood what I'd done wrong. That was much more useful.'

After a few more months of testing with her grandmother's neighbours, Maya put Next Door online. At first only a handful of families in her street joined, but then a local radio station interviewed her, and the number of users grew almost overnight. Today the app is used in towns all over the country.

Several companies have since offered to buy Next Door, but Maya has turned them all down. 'They wanted to add advertising and charge people to use it,' she says. 'The people who need it most are often the ones with the least money, so that's not going to happen.'

Maya admits it hasn't always been easy to balance the app with her schoolwork, especially during exams. She now spends only Sunday afternoons on it, and a small team of volunteers answers users' messages during the week.

Her advice for other young people with an idea is simple. 'Don't wait until you feel ready, because you never will. Start with something small, and expect it to go wrong. That's how you learn.'

passages.title: Small steps to healthier eating
passages.text:
Most of us know we should eat more fruit and vegetables, but changing the way we eat is not always easy. Experts say the secret is to (1) ______ small changes, one at a time, rather than trying to change everything at once.

For example, instead of (2) ______ breakfast because you are in a hurry, try preparing something the night before. A bowl of porridge with some fresh fruit will (3) ______ you full of energy until lunchtime, and you will be less likely to buy biscuits or crisps during the morning.

It is also a good idea to (4) ______ attention to how much sugar there is in the food you buy. Many products which are (5) ______ as healthy, such as fruit yoghurts and cereal bars, actually contain a surprising amount of it. Reading the labels carefully in the supermarket only takes a few minutes.

Finally, try not to eat your meals in front of the television or your phone. When your mind is on something else, it is easy to eat far more than you need without (6) ______ it.
